speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have the pleasure to present a petition signed by 279 constituents of Kingston and the Islands who protest the closure of VTA Rail as contemplated in the cuts announced by the Government in the recent Budget.

Petitions
The petitioners indicate that they believe the railroad was established as a national system in the last century and has played an integral part in the growth of Canada, that the loss of jobs will be a significant loss for the countiy. Many communities rely on rail service as their primary means of transportation.
They call upon Parliament to urge the Government not to cancel in whole or in part VIA Rail passenger service across Canada.

Madam Speaker, I too have the honour to present a petition pursuant to Standing Order 36 regarding the Government's intention to close down all or part of VIA Rail.
The petitioners from western Canada point out the very critical role that VIA plays in the development of the economy of western Canada, particularly the development of the tourist sector there.
They are asking Parliament to maintain, improve, and modernize VIA Rail service as opposed to cutting it back and give a whole set of reasons as to why it would be in the best interest of the country.

Madam Speaker, I also have another petition on a different topic. Again it is certified correct pursuant to Standing Order 36.
It points out the Government's involvement in ARMX '89, the arms bazaar currently being held in the nation's capital. It illustrates the Government's support for the growing militarization of our Canadian economy.
The petitioners also point out that the potential customers at this exhibit, those who have received special invitations, include countries which have habitually violated the human rights of their citizens. They point out that military spending of course diverts material and human resources from more important economic activities and social programs.
They call upon Parliament to cease all government involvement in the expansion of the international market for military and policing equipment, particularly the Government's support of ARMX '89.

Madam Speaker, I have two petitions to present from people in my riding. The first quotes the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada which said: "The federal Government has the responsibility to ensure that rail passenger services in Canada be retained, modernized, and expanded as an important part of our national transportation system".
The petitioners point out that the Government has failed to live up to its original pledge to support VIA Rail. They call on the Government to abandon its plans to cut back VIA's budget and to provide the necessary resources to allow VIA to operate as a modem, effective transportation company rather than as a museum.

Madam Speaker, my second petition calls upon the Government not to sign the Order in Council which would remove oats from the marketing jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board, and to place oats and barley under the Wheat Board Act in such a way that in future farm organizations and the Parliament of Canada must be consulted before changes are made to the marketing of these products.

Madam Speaker, it is my honour and duty in accordance with Standing Order 36 to present several petitions which have been duly certified by the Clerk.
The first is a petition from a number of residents of Newfoundland who point out that in Guatemala bombing, torture, disappearances, and murders of the civilian population are increasing.
They call upon Parliament to direct the Government to stop all government to government aid to Guatemala and not to renew it until there is a genuine end to the war between the Government of Guatemala and its own citizens.

Madam Speaker, I have another petition from about 300 persons mainly in the City of Toronto who are concerned with the uncertainty about the Government's programs for dealing with the refugee backlog that came about in the last few years.
They point out that there will be a great many of them who may be denied the opportunity to stay in Canada through inadequate hearings of the merits either of their
May 23, 1989

refugee case or of their plea for humanitarian consideration.
They ask the House to ensure that the Minister of Employment and Immigration will ensure that those who have notified Canada Immigration of their intention to make a claim will all be considered eligible for immediate employment authorizations and a case by case review of their claims.
The review should include humanitarian and compassionate grounds traditionally used by Canada Immigration, including the presence in Canada of relatives, the successful establishment of refugee claimants in Canada, and special consideration being given to those coming from war zones, oppressive Governments and natural disasters.

Therefore, they pray that Parliament will ensure that the Government and Parliament act to bring such an amendment in as specified above with all due haste and speed.

Has the government taken steps to ensure that the movement of funds between sub-programs in its Direct Delivery component of the Canada -British Columbia Forest Resource Development Agreement receives ministerial approval and, if so, what are they?

speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Forestry)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Forestry)
speechtext:
Under the Canada-British Columbia Forest Resource Development Agreement (FRDA), the two governments established three management committees based on the delivery stream (cost-shared, federal direct, provincial direct) which are responsible to the provincial Minister of Forestry and the federal Minister of State (Forestry) for implementation of the Agreement.
The re-allocation of funds between programs requires ministerial approval and an amendment to the legal agreement. However, the legal agreement further stipulates that each of the three Management Committees may move funds from one sub-program to another, but only within the same program. In the present case, the management Committee for the Agreement has the authority to move funds between sub-programs in the direct delivery component and does not require ministe-
May 23, 1989

rial approval. As this Management Committee has the authority to make these adjustments as required, ministerial approval has not been necessary.
The intent of this provision is to provide the Management Committees with sufficient flexibility to respond to operational constraints as well as opportunities. This flexibility in management helps to ensure the most efficient use of government funds, while at the same time guaranteeing that Ministers retain absolute control.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACTOF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACTOF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
That this House condemns the Government for its destructive policies affecting Canadian farmers, that have particularly devastating impact on the dairy, grain, horticulture and tobacco sectors, that undermine supply management agencies such as the Canadian Wheat Board and marketing boards at both the federal and provincial levels, and that break government promises relating to 1988 drought payments; and
That this House calls upon the Government to fulfil immediately its promises with regard to drought payments for the 1988-89 crop year, to implement a contingency plan for the current crop year, in view of indications of another drought in Western Canada, and to reverse its policies that are destroying the Canadian supply management system.
He said: Madam Speaker, I rise today in the House to attempt to address the Government's record in agriculture and the uncertainty resulting from that record, an uncertainty which the Government should address immediately.
This record shows a catering to big agri-business, a catering to foreign interests, and a real failure to address many of the concerns facing the people they should be serving. These people are tilling the land as we speak in
Supply
this House of Commons, the Canadian farmers who are involved in their spring planting at this point.
The primary producers are the first but not the least important link in the food chain. It is sad that in a world where millions of people are starving farmers are being forced off their land because they do not make enough return to pay their bills.
As I examine the agricultural record of the Government, I notice that there appears to have been a shift away from the proven and traditional marketing systems, systems that may have been of a different ideology than that of the Government. However, that shift is a shift in priority. No longer does the Government take the farmer as its number one priority.
The Government is wearing horse blinders, running wild, oblivious to those whose policies are being trampled and those whose concerns it is passing.
By examining sector by sector today, by myself and my esteemed colleagues, this side of the House will make it clear to the people of Canada what too many farmers already know, that agricultural concerns are being sacrificed for the FEA.
Last summer farmers across Canada were hit hard by a severe drought. Now they are being hard hit by the Tory Government.
Farmers were promised by none other than the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds that they would be compensated for their losses at a rate of $40 to $45 an acre of wheat in Western Canada and $50 to $57 per acre of com and beans in the East for a total pay-out of roughly $850 million. Further, the Minister promised that this $850 million was simply an estimate and not a ceiling.
When we have seen and heard about all of the hardships that Canadian farmers have experienced these last few years, we would think that it would be a top priority of any Government to lessen the blow. As Canadians we pride ourselves in taking care of our farmers through the use of such mechanisms as marketing boards, compensation programs, and stabilization.
However, where is the compassion of the Government? Where are its priorities? They are certainly not with the Canadian farmers.

May 23, 1989
Supply
I have good reason for questioning the sincerity of the Government and its commitment to farmers. Just look at the Estimates tabled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) for drought relief, Madam Speaker. They do not read $850 million. They read approximately $378 million plus another $30 million in Governor General warrants.
What has happened since the election? Does this Government believe it was given a mandate to change the rules of the game so that immediately after an election it could force the provinces to come up with an extra $425 million to pay for a federal election promise? I am not sure how the provinces could be expected to pay for an election promise of any kind. What do I tell the farmers in my riding and across Canada who are planting their crops, who have their bills to pay and were counting on drought compensation cheques from the Government?
I just hope the Government is not delaying its payments scheduled for July. The farmers were promised that money. They have bills to pay and their need is desperate.
The Minister set a deadline of 13 days from the announcement for returning applications for assistance under the drought relief program. What if an appropriate number of those producers are still attempting to receive applications? What are they going to do? This action, however, fails to surprise me any more than the continuing delays in the program. I cannot overemphasize the gravity of the situation. Farmers hit hard by drought do not need this kind of delay treatment by government. They need the help they were promised, and they need it now.
I would like now to address the concerns of the wheat producers of Canada. We know from the United States trade representative's report to Congress that it is the intent of the U.S. Government to eliminate the licensing practices of the Canadian Wheat Board. It is not hard to surmise that Canada's Wheat Board marketing will be eliminated to appease the U.S.
Last Thursday I read that the United States Department of Agriculture will approve further subsidies on 1.5 million tonnes of wheat destined for the Soviet Union. These subsidies amount to about 28 cents per bushel. This will subsidize the United States grain exports to the tune of almost $13 million U.S. For the benefit of those Members across the floor, that is almost $15 million
Canadian. The Americans are continuing on with their subsidies through the Export Enhancement Program.
In view of the fact the U.S. President has reauthorized the Export Enhancement Program, I ask that the Government tell us when the producers in this country will get the much heralded level playing field.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACTOF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext: Never!

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACTOF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
According to the Ontario Wheat Producer Marketing Board if a foreign importer buys United States wheat the final price is reduced by $30 a tonne. At the world price of $180 per tonne, the Ontario farmer must offer his wheat for sale at $150 per tonne in order to attempt to sell to that buyer on equal grounds. That is not taking into account the loss due to the lower value of our dollar.
In addition to this reduction of $30 per tonne, a farmer in St. Clair County, Michigan, can get up to three tonnes of ammonium nitrate fertilizer free if he has 40 acres of wheat. That is 150 pounds per acre free from his local supplier. Of course the United States says that this is not a producer subsidy, but it is an indirect subsidy to the producer and we as Canadians must compete against it. Yet, the Government has unilaterally disarmed our wheat producers and has thrown them to the vagaries of the market-place and the laws of the jungle.
There is another problem facing the wheat industry that to date the Government has refused to address, namely, the policy of end user certificates. End user certificates will be required when the level of subsidy between each country reaches a level that will permit the free flow of grains across the border. The difficulty of which I am confident the Government is aware is that end users certificates will not require the grade of wheat to be identified. This allows for the import of low grade wheat at lower prices than that of Canadian wheat. This is due to the quality of the control disparities which breed unfair competition, and believe me a few truckloads of low quality, ungraded wheat can destroy a stable price structure such as we have in Canada.
I would like to leave Canadian wheat for the moment and turn to oats. Again, we find the Government's record to be questionable. This past Wednesday the Canadian Wheat Board admitted what Members on this side of the House contended all along, that the lower initial prices for wheat are due to the Free Trade Agreement and the Government's fear of being placed

on the U.S. trade representative's Super 310 list, about which I will say more later.
Last in this area we have the Government's decision to remove oats from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board arbitrarily. This action broke the Government's own Citizen Code of Regulatory Fairness. This code was established by the Members opposite with much fanfare in March 1986, and the Government claims that it consulted with the producers. The polls show that 63 per cent of the producers were against the removal and 75 per cent were upset at not being consulted. Given the substantial list of pools and others who have voted to condemn the action, I wonder how the Government managed to come up with a consultation process that was selective enough to get the response it wanted. Perhaps it was the same source that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) used to determine that VIA Rail ridership was only 20 per cent.
While only about 1 per cent of oats are handled by the Canadian Wheat Board, this is the thin edge of the wedge. I should clarify that. Only 1 per cent of the volume handled by the Canadian Wheat Board is made up of oats. Because the level of subsidies on oats will be equal between Canada and the United States this year, the Minister removed oats from the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board as called for under the Free Trade Agreement. Forecasts are that wheat and barley subsidies will be equal in about a year. Will they also be removed from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board when that time comes?
I ask the Government to tell Canadian farmers just what will be the role of the Canadian Wheat Board and the Ontario Wheat Board when free trade in wheat takes effect next year. A major end-user of grains told me less than a month ago that the Canadian Wheat Board will be out of business within two years. That is shocking. It is unacceptable to the farmers of Canada.
Another agricultural sector that was hard hit just a few weeks ago was the pork producers. During last fall's election campaign, Canadians were told time and time again about how the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement was supposed to guarantee access to the United States market. We on this side of the House argued that this access has not been guaranteed and that the United
Supply
States can still hurt us with countervailing duties whenever and however it sees fit, because its trade remedy laws are still intact and Canadians are not exempted.
Listen to some of the words of a Conservative advertisement which appeared last fall: "The Free Trade Agreement guarantees that Canadian farmers will have an open U.S. market for beef and pork". Another candidate from southwestern Ontario said: "the Free 'Trade Agreement is making sure that we are able to trade in the United States and not have to worry about countervailing of products that are moving right now". Canadian farmers would not have to worry about countervail. I am afraid those are famous last words because on May 3, 1989, a headline in The Globe and Mail stated that the United States attacks Canadian subsidies and ups the ante for imported pork. On May 4, 1989, another headline stated that pork duty troubles Canadian farmers.
Why are Canadian farmers troubled? I thought the Government, clutching to its Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, was supposed to eradicate these kinds of worries for farmers. The facts lead us to believe that this is not the case. Not one week after the Free Trade Agreement was put into effect, the U.S. pork industry filed a petition maintaining that according to the United States, Canadian pork producers benefit from more than 20 potential subsidy programs, including market price guarantees and drought payments.
Subsequently, a duty of 7.7 cents per kilogram was slapped on Canadian pork exports. I realize that this money is placed in bond pending a final decision, but the fact is producers' prices dropped immediately this announcement was made. This is money out of the pockets of pork producers.
A final decision will be made by the United States Commerce Department on July 17 as to whether or not the 7.7 cents per kilogram duty on Canadian pork will be maintained. I urge the Government to defend the interests of Canadian pork producers and to refuse to allow the U.S. Government to call into question some of the most essential and vital aspects of agriculture in Canada today.
The Government has been slashing programs left and right, mostly to the right, and giving in to the United States Government to such an extent that pork produc-

May 23, 1989
Supply
ers are not only getting fried by the Government but are getting burned.
Of course, we have to look at what is happening to the Canadian dairy industry. The recent response by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Mazankowski) to the GATT-Dunkel Agreement has confirmed what we on this side of the House have suspected ever since we first read the Free Trade Agreement. The Members on this side know what it says. We realize that the Government does not recognize the simple fact that once the cows are out, it is too late to close the bam door, that one should always negotiate from a position of strength and that one does not throw the baby out with the bathwater.
First, the intent of the interim GATT agreement that will go down in infamy as the Dunkel Agreement was to limit and decrease the incentives that subsidies create that result in over-production. At the same time, the Government continues to claim to stand by and to be defending producer-controlled marketing under GATT Article XI. What then was the Government's response to Dunkel? It was to place a cap on the very mechanism that the Government announced last January as the saviour of the industrial milk industry.
As anyone who can see could tell us, it is as plain as day that support prices on Canadian products have no impact on exports and certainly no effect on the intent of Dunkel. Indeed, the dairy producers pay for the disposal of over-production themselves. These support prices are totally permissible under GATT Article XI. Clearly, the message is that either the Government does not know how to negotiate and does not understand Article XI of GATT, or does not care about producer-controlled marketing.
If milk prices rise, this program will bring about the type of pricing that is the goal of the Government's Advisory Council on Adjustment. Second, the Government is currently under fire at GATT for including ice cream and yoghurt on the import control list. The United States Government is trying to argue that ice cream and yoghurt are not products like milk and that it is not necessary to have border controls in order to support a producer-managed marketing system. I understand that we have only a 50-50 chance of winning, but if we do not win this case, the precedent will be set and it
will open a floodgate for other products and other commodities.
Both you and I, Madam Speaker, can clearly see that ice cream is like yoghurt and like milk. The only logic that can support this decision is the same logic the Government used to argue during the election campaign that chicken parts are not chicken. I have a copy of a section of the Free Hade Agreement that I would like to read. It deals with how chicken cannot be chicken. I would like to read it, because if I do not, I do not believe that the Canadian public would believe it. Annex 706 talks about market access for poultry and reads:
Without limiting the generality of subparagraph 1(a), chicken and chicken products does not include chicken cordon bleu, breaded breast of chicken cordon bleu, chicken Kiev, breaded breast of chicken Kiev, boneless Rock Cornish with rice, stuffed Rock Cornish, boneless chicken with apples and almonds, chicken Romanoff Regell, chicken Neptune breast, boneless chicken Panache, chicken TV dinners, old roosters, and "spent fowl" commonly called "stewing hen".
It goes on to list processed turkey which is not considered to be turkey. How in the world can we believe the logic of the Government when it opens up the borders to such large volumes of products that can take advantage of this clause in the years ahead?
I call on the Government to demand that GATT reject this logic out of hand. More important is the fact that the Government has not acted quickly and decisively to challenge the second United States contention. If the Government allows the United States to enforce the belief that import controls are an unnecessary part of a producer-controlled marketing system, then the whole reasoning behind such a system will become obsolete. How can there be measures to ensure that there is not over-production in one country if its neighbours can export their over-production at will?
It must be recognized that producer marketing is part of the solution to world over-production, certainly not part of the problem. What has the Government opposite done to ensure that this right is not lost, to ensure the future of our producer marketing system, a system that is the best in the world and is envied around the world? Has it stood up to the American negotiators and exposed the multitude of hidden indirect subsidies that are available to United States' farmers through feed companies, grain elevators, fertilizer companies and the Commodity Credit Corporation? Has the Government confronted United States negotiators with the fact that a
May 23, 1989

dairy farmer in St. Clair County, Michigan, with 44 cows, will receive roughly $10,000 worth of free feed, $10,000 worth of Commodity Credit Corporation com? Surely this has to be considered a subsidy.
Finally, I might ask why the Government has not challenged at GATT the U.S.'s own practices in regard to ice cream. The United States has failed for 17 years to file a report on the U.S. quota which is to be established yearly on a proportional basis. Further, the Government should ask why that quota has not been met and why it was not opened to other countries like Canada, as GATT rules stipulate. The answer to all these questions is not very hard to determine.
During the free trade debate Members on this side of the House argued passionately, and now would appear correctly, that the agricultural interests in Canada were sacrificed to get a Free Trade Agreement with the United States, that agricultural subsidies were not allowed but that subsidies in other industries were, such as energy. I have here the final text of the FTA, Article 906. Under Article 906 it states:
Both Parties have agreed to allow existing or future incentives for oil and gas exploration, development and related activities in order to maintain the reserve base for these energy resources.
This deal has imposed a double standard on Canadian farmers. The Government is making them second class citizens and has bargained away their marketing systems and their livelihoods. Did the U.S. Government object to the subsidy? If not, why then did the Government not get the same rights for agriculture? The Americans need our oil and gas. Certainly they are not going to object to our Canadian taxpayers subsidizing something they need. Believe me, the Canadian people will be paying through the nose for their own energy until it runs out.
Recently the Government introduced a Budget that holds title to many firsts. It was the first televised Budget. It was the first Budget to be pre-released. It was the first Budget to spawn an RCMP investigation. It is important to note that this Budget, mishandled as it was, was also the first free trade Budget. This was a Conservative budgetary future, a free trade budget that fingers for elimination the items that our government agreed
Supply
with the United States to be considered to be unfair subsidies.
There have been cuts in stabilization programs, cuts in transport programs affecting farmers, cuts in crop insurance, cuts in farm credit, cuts in fuel rebates, cuts in interest relief as well as the elimination of the special Canadian grains program, despite the fact that there is only a lull in the war, not a cessation of hostilities. This included a $14 million loss to the dairy industry. It has been estimated that this Budget will cost every farmer in Canada at least $1,000 each per year.
The answers to the questions I have raised today are not so much pointing to the FTA, but to the fact that the Members opposite not only negotiated to get a deal at any cost, but now that they have the deal they will do anything to keep it, anything to say we have access to the American market, anything to say that Canada is not being treated like other U.S. trading partners.
On the last day of May, a United States trade representative will present United States Congress with a list of countries that are viewed by them as having unfair barriers to American imports. The countries on the list that do not remove those barriers within 18 months will be retaliated against by the United States with tariffs and sanctions. To date, the trade representative has cited Canadian practices which it considers unfair regarding restrictions on advertising, discriminatory postal rates, plywood, alcoholic beverages, the dairy industry, poultry, and wheat, the dairy industry, poultry and wheat being looked upon as having unfair trading practices. The United States trade representative did not even mention the pork industry, which I discussed earlier and which is currently suffering retaliatory countervails from the United States.
We have a great country, Madam Speaker, made great by the sweat of our forefathers who tilled the earth and cleared the land. We as Members have to ensure that the heritage is not lost and the farmers of this nation have an income commensurate with the rest of society.

He talked about Article 11 and the protection of the dairy farmer and the poultry farmer in Canada. I am wondering what he has got against

He will know that under this Government, farm income is the highest it has ever been. He will recognize that this Government has supported agriculture in a way that no other government ever has. He spoke himself about 17 years of neglect by the Americans, 17 years that encompassed the period that his Government was in power, three months of which was when he was Minister of Agriculture. Now we are with the GATT agreements trying to reinforce it. What does he have against these people that he would want us not to reinforce and to clarify Article 11 of GATT?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACTOF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, perhaps I have to go back a few years to when some of the marketing boards were first being formed. They were brought about by the need for a countervailing force in the market place, a countervailing force that is utilized by the producers. Perhaps I had better tell you how long I have been involved. It will be 40 years ago next December when, as a teenager, I was asked to sit as a township committee man on one of the local marketing boards.
I well remember the problems we experienced before that time. There had to be some different mechanism put in place so that the farmer could have a return on investment and labour in order to meet his payments. That situation is not unlike what we have at the present time, as there appears to be a move to tear these apart. But I also want to reflect back on the other marketing boards that I have been involved in at township levels over the years, such as wheat, the Ontario Pork Producers Marketing Board, later on with Eggs and then with TUrkeys and Broilers. Over the years we decided there had to be a better way. It is only with the implementation of the legislation to create the National Farm Producers Marketing Act in early 1972 that these mechanisms were
put in the hands of the producers so they could have control over their own destiny and tailor their production to the needs of the Canadian consumer and provide that consumer with a high quality product at a reasonable cost.
These are the things that have been put into place through the enabling legislation and they have proved very successful. We had the Canadian Wheat Board established well before the National Farm Products Marketing Agencies were brought into effect. The Canadian Wheat Board was brought into place to ensure that the farmers had the best possible return in the marketplace.
Now we see those systems being challenged, even though the eggs were challenged under GATT several years ago when the National Egg Marketing Plan was brought into effect. We won that challenge because of the precedent set under Article 11. We want to make sure that that challenge is not brought up again. I am afraid it may be brought up and we will only have a 50-50 chance of winning. So it is in this context that I want to support our national and provincial marketing systems across this nation. With the concentration of power in the market-place, with the huge corporations, with the buying clubs that supply about 70 per cent of food at the retail food level, the farmers themselves have to be able to establish their price at the farm gate, a price that reflects the cost of the production with a reasonable return on investment and labour.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring a western voice to this debate. Agriculture is important to western Canada. It is important to all of Canada. We really are not very happy about that. We needed that money very badly".
Despite the impatience of the Minister across the aisle, I wanted to point out that farmers in Manitoba and throughout the West are extremely upset with the manner in which the Government has handled the Drought Assistance Program. Not only does it appear that the Government has not set aside enough money, that is, enough of what was promised, but the manner in which it has been handled is a disaster.
Does the Hon. Member realize how steamed up the farmers are, particularly those in western Canada?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACTOF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
I do indeed realize how steamed up the farmers are in western Canada, and rightfully so. On my last trip out there I interviewed a lot of farmers and members of farm organizations. I also flew over some of the prairie areas and noticed that the dugouts were empty. Even though there seemed to be an adequate snow cover, the subsoil moisture reserves were simply not there. Such is the case at the present time in many areas of southwestern Ontario.
I do want to indicate the immediate and essential need for those payments to be put in the hands of the farmers. A farmer is an eternal optimist. He always looks ahead to a good crop every year, regardless of the returns last year. When the Government decides that a rain stops at a township or county line and does not go across the border and one fellow gets it and another does not, that indicates there is something dramatically wrong. There has to be something better. If this situation occurs again, there has to be a different type of administration or a different way of administration so that we can have more accurate records.

They volunteered to go up and down the concessions and call on the farmers to ask them who had proper yield records and moisture records and, in turn, were able to determine new areas that should have been included in the initial maps.
I certainly concur with my hon. colleague from Manitoba that it is essential that this money be put in the hands of producers as quickly as possible.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACTOF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson) has a short or selective memory. He has forgotten that when he was Minister of Agriculture in 1984 that the dairy farmers of Canada had waited four to five years for a long-term dairy policy that was put in place by this Conservative Government. The Hon. Member was in office as a Minister, and he has forgotten. We do not have any lessons to learn from that Member on the drought. There was a drought in Quebec in 1983. As a Member of Parliament from that area, Madam Speaker, I am sure that you were aware there were rough times during the drought in 1983. The dairy farmers and all the farmers of Canada remember that.

Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in today's debate on Canadian agriculture. I am convinced that at the end of the day, Canadians will realize once again that this Government defends the interests of the agri-food industry. Madam Speaker, I think that this Government, more than any other, has given farmers a helping hand during the past four years and is still doing so at the beginning of its new term.
We realize how important the agri-food sector is to Canada and to the economy of this country. We have always been prepared to defend this sector in the past and we continue to do so. Every time farmers needed a helping hand, we have given them that helping hand. I can prove it! During the past four years, Madam Speaker, we have invested over $17 billion in Canadian
agriculture, and we have taken the necessary steps to protect the basic mechanisms of that agriculture.
For instance, quite recently, we added yoghurt and ice cream to the items on the Import Control List, for the purpose of protecting the dairy supply management system in this country.
Madam Speaker, also quite recently, we introduced import controls for broiler hatching eggs. We would never have done so if we were not willing to strengthen this country's agricultural roots.
Some people, however, are inclined to doubt that. Strengthening the foundation of a sector that often leads a troubled existence, with fluctuating market prices and fluctuating weather, is not particularly easy. It is a daily challenge, both for farmers and for governments.
However, Madam Speaker, you know as well as I do that challenge does not necessarily mean difficulty. However, that is what some people would have farmers believe. Others go even further to suggest that the present Government has been destructive in the measures that it has taken with respect to agriculture, as reflected in today's motion and in the comments we have heard during the last few weeks.
There are also those who try to scare farmers by claiming that some sectors will be sacrificed for the sake of the survival and development of others. Nothing could be farther from the truth, Madam Speaker!
This confusion, augmented by many Members of the Opposition, makes it incumbent on me, Madam Speaker, to set the record straight, especially with respect to dairy supply management, a subject to which I am very close and on which I have worked for a number of years.
On April 7, member countries negotiating at the GATT talks agreed on a framework for negotiations that will make it possible for them to complete these difficult talks by December 1990.
To keep the international trade situation from deteriorating during the next 20 months, all member countries-not just Canada but all member countries-have agreed to a truce, in other words, a short-term capping
May 23, 1989

in the agricultural sector. This means, Madam Speaker, that member countries have agreed that subsidized prices, which are set above international prices, will not exceed present levels.
For countries like Canada who want changes in international trade in agricultural products, it is a first step that was long overdue, considering the urgency of the situation.
Most Hon. Members will recall the fervour and intensity with which our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) defended, at all economic summits in recent years, the need for ending this senseless agricultural trade war. So this ceiling to which the countries have agreed is in keeping with our Government's clear, unwavering commitment to maintain supply management, because we believe that continued cooperation with our trading partners will give more weight to Article XI, which was mentioned a few minutes ago.
Indeed, Madam Speaker, that is how I think this agreement reached on April 7 must be considered-as real progress for the Canadian dairy industry and all the country's farmers. The short-term agreements reached in Geneva have somewhat broken the deadlock that was blocking multilateral trade negotiations and prevented significant progress from being achieved at the meeting in Montreal last December.
This cease-fire is an undeniable advantage for Canadian dairy farmers who want GATT Article XI maintained and strengthened. Since we can now deal with the actual reform of international agricultural trade, we can specify the types of commodities, under that famous Article XI, which can be subject to import controls as part of supply management. For example, for the dairy sector, we will make rules to allow import controls for some dairy products. We did not hesitate in the past, Madam Speaker, to add products to this list, in the interests of Canadian farmers, and if the need arises in future, we will never hesitate to do so.
I believe that we shall also try to specify the minimum requirements to be met by a supply management system so that clear import controls can be imposed under Article XI. Canadian dairy farmers will thus obtain protection from potential misuse by some of our trading partners of provisions of Article XI such as import restrictions.
Supply
Canadian dairy farmers, Madam Speaker, have helped us maintain Article XI by working with farmers from other countries and explaining to them the advantages of such a mechanism.
I hope they will continue their efforts in this respect and thus help to strengthen our position in trade talks at the international level. I know Canada's dairy producers understand this process and this policy and that they appreciate its merits. Because of international tension and the kind of trench warfare being waged by certain countries in the international arena of agricultural trade, it is so important to provide information instead of succumbing to scare tactics and closing our minds to reason.
Madam Speaker, there are those who ridicule our efforts and criticize our actions, claiming that Canadian dairy producers should not be bound by this international agreement since they only produce for the domestic market.
However, even if our supply management system is such that our dairy producers contribute very little to world dairy surpluses, the fact remains, Madam Speaker, that a certain amount of our dairy products is exported.
Last year, for instance, we exported $191 million worth of dairy products, and most of those sales were at prices below the price on the Canadian domestic market. For the dairy year 1988-89, production is expected to exceed the market-sharing quota by 4 per cent, which surplus will be entirely exported, in addition to the 3 per cent of intra-quota production already earmarked for export.
Furthermore, Madam Speaker, incomes of Canadian dairy producers are also partly determined by international price levels. For instance, the world price for skim milk powder has tripled in the last five years, which has helped to reduce levies on payments to producers. Canadian dairy producers were thus able to absorbs more easily the cost of marketing skim milk for export.
In fact, the increase in world prices brought about by the changes certain countries made in their domestic policies, as a result of pressure for international reform of agricultural trade, exercised by Canada, for instance, has helped Canadian dairy producers save more than $70 million last year alone, compared to 1986. This represents about $1.50 or even more than or per hectolitre. This is money in the pockets of agricultural producers and Canadian dairy producers! And this shows that taking positive action on the international market for

Supply
greater discipline among those concerned has a direct effect on the Canadian dairy fanner's pocketbook. This must be recognized by all partners.
Our dairy farmers, like all Canadian farmers, have everything to gain from fair trade rules that permit reduced export support by other countries and thus strengthen world market prices.
I know that the Government is accused of not keeping its 1986 commitment on the long-term dairy policy. Nevertheless, Madam Speaker, we implemented this long-term dairy policy because our friends, and my colleague from Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson) who was just speaking was Minister of Agriculture in 1984- He had every opportunity. He was part of a government that could have implemented a long-term dairy policy, but it remained in limbo for many years. What did he do? Nothing! We implemented it in 1986, and the $6.03 per hectolitre for domestic consumption for processed milk producers remains in place and is worth $275 million a year for Canadian farmers. That is a lot of money, Madam Speaker.
Once again we are being accused of abandoning dairy producers because the short term capping of farm support would not make it possible for us to live up to the production cost formula. Now, Madam Speaker, let us look at facts. For the time being, whether we like it or not, we just cannot determine what the production costs will be as per the formula the next time we use it this summer. We must collect all the data concerning production costs, producers' efficiency, so that later on this summer we will have the correct figures. This is somewhat an hypothetical issue. We just cannot determine for the time being the impact of the truce on the targeted revenues from industrial milk and cream. My colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, clearly indicated that should the current situation dramatically change when the production costs are calculated, the Government, which has always held a responsible position, will do again the right thing and consider appropriate measures, just as it has always done in the past.
Canadian dairy producers, something our hon. colleagues in the Opposition should acknowledge, are well aware that on two occasions, in August 1988 and February of this year, the Federal Government decided not to lower the targeted price for industrial milk in spite of the expected results had the formula been applied. This would have meant a reduction of $1.89 the hectolitre of milk in August 1988, and a further reduction of 14 cents in February 1989. The Government had then recognized that last year's drought had had a fairly direct impact on the increase of feed price in a number of regions. We had therefore done the right thing for which we have yet to receive praise from our colleagues opposite, by maintaining the targeted prices for industrial milk at the levels reached at the time.
It is clear, therefore, that when all the facts are taken into account and analyzed objectively, this Government's commitment to dairy producers is beyond question. The facts are undeniable. They easily stand up to any partial or biased review. Therefore, those who believe that our supply management systems, especially in the case of dairy products, are being bargained away so that other Canadian farm products can more easily gain access to export markets are totally wrong. The truce applies to all countries, all farm products and all policies. And it is certainly not, Madam Speaker, as some dare claim, a scheme to use new international commitments as an excuse to cut Canadian farming support. All these allegations that have been heard these past few weeks are pure speculations and do not bear any resemblance with reality.
I would like, Madam Speaker, to end my comments on the motion being examined by discussing the Budget and its impact on agriculture. I said at the beginning of my speech that the federal government tried to reinforce the foundations of Canadian agriculture. The last Budget does not defeat this purpose. Essentially, the Budget reduces government expenditure that affect a series of programs from national defence to government operating activities.
We had to make difficult choices. In fact, we tried to ensure that the budgetary measures as a whole were balanced, that they reflected regional realities and that they transfered a part of the debt burden to those who were in a position to assume it. These are difficult choices, but as a government, as the managers of this
May 23, 1989

In resuming the remarks that I had intended to make, Madam Speaker, I am pleased that the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson) put forward this motion because it gives us all a chance to review the agricultural policy before the country today.
I was a little taken aback, I suppose, when I did not hear in the Hon. Member's remarks any off-setting solutions to the farm problem. In fact, during the election campaign I did not hear from the Liberal Party any proposals that would solve the farm problem. I have to admit that during the election campaign we did not hear anything from the Government either. The only policy it had was, "If you need it, we will provide it. Just trust us". Trust us, trust us, trust us became the focus of the whole agricultural policy.
There are an awful lot of farmers in farm communities in rural areas of this country who are finding that "trust us" is not good enough. TTiey want to know what the long-term direction is from the various parties and they want to know it now because they are making plans to either leave agriculture or stay in it.
In my part of the country, the Prairies, we have seen 28,000 farm jobs disappear under this "trust us" policy in the last year. Market towns that have been market towns since the coming of settlers to Western Canada are at the point at which it is impossible to get farm machinery supplies, parts, services and new equipment because they can no longer support that particular service in a town with a population of 1,500 to 5,000. The City of Melville in Saskatchewan, a town of 5,000 souls, no longer has a farm equipment dealership. Apparently, there is not enough money in the area to support a farm equipment dealership. That situation has arisen under this Government, even with the assistance that has been given.
Farmers and their lenders and the community that provides supporting services have to have more assurances as to where they stand in the scheme of things in the Government's economic order. The New Democratic Party proposed that it was time to institute the kinds of programs that we see in a lot of competing countries. Even though the focus of international talks is to reducing subsidies, our country is in a very vulnerable position by going into a reduced subsidy kind of mode.
Our subsidies are mostly up front in the form of ad hoc payments, which can be easily dropped. We do not have that many long-term commitments to subsidize farmers or to provide economic underpinnings to them. So, when you start deregulating agriculture and pulling the subsidies away, if that is not done very carefully on a proportionate basis we will find ourselves operating with no support from the rest of the country and still competing against countries like the United States and the European Economic Community that are still using a great deal of taxpayers' money to keep their farmers and rural communities in business.
I know there are ideologues in the Conservative Party who say, "If the market will not support them, then there is no reason for farmers in rural communities to exist". They have started down the road to complete market orientation with their deregulation program they have picked up from the Liberals and carried on throughout the Government's last mandate. That means that transportation costs in rural areas will no longer be cross-subsidized with those in the metropolitan areas. It also means that we in the rural areas will be paying more for services such as delivery' of parts, postal service and moving our grain and livestock because rail and trucking rates have been deregulated. It means that institutions like the Canadian Wheat Board and other marketing boards are now under scrutiny by the Government. The Government says this is not a true market economy, that boards are a form of near monopoly and do not reflect the kind of market that this Government thinks should exist. So it is deregulating those marketing boards.
Western Canadian farmers will understand this because as of August 1 this year oats will no longer be part of the Canadian Wheat Board system. Farmers will be taking slightly less money for their oats in the coming crop year. That is borne out not just by my analysis but the analysis of Canadian processors. I have discussed this issue with several of them. They say it was a good decision because they can buy oats cheaper. When I asked the processors if this means farmers will get less money, they said, "Of course. How else do we get oats for less money?" The Government thinks it is good for farmers to take home less money. But I do not. Most Canadians who look at it fairly do not think so either.
May 23, 1989

But because it is a form of deregulation and leaves more product to the open market, this Government has decided to pursue that particular policy.
We have seen changes to the taxation system that are supposed to be more market oriented. This last Budget which was leaked all over the place before it was finally presented to the public in general has a provision which states that at the end of this calendar year the rebates on farm fuel taxation will stop. This will cost farmers considerably more money for fuel. Farmers have to cover great distances, most of them being located quite a long way from metropolitan areas, so the increase will add not only to the cost of farming operations but to the cost of moving product to markets as well. This leaves less for the family on the farm to spend on expansion, maintenance and living expenses.
I think that points out the need for some guidelines or rules to provide a certain amount of assistance that will be there in good times or bad times, a program that will exist decade to decade so that rural areas will know what the rules are vis-a-vis their subsistence and government funds.
During the election campaign, we proposed a system of providing minimum guaranteed prices on a certain level of production so that farmers and their communities would know that there would be a certain level of money coming in for the first units of production. We proposed that it be about 8,000 production units which would be equivalent to about 8,000 bushels of wheat or a little over 10,000 bushels of com. The idea was to provide a price guarantee in the neighbourhood of $40,000 per farm family so that regardless of how bad the market was, farm families could rely on at least that much for the first units of production. When prices would rise, it would not cost the taxpaying public any money because the market would take care of the problem.
We do not have very many of those kinds of systems left in place because we have deregulated and have become more market oriented. What is the rationale for our kind of program? It is very simple. We have done comparisons of rural economies in various parts of the world and have found that where we can keep active units in the rural economy at the small family level, the local economy thrives. When the production in an area is carried out by large corporate entities, the community dies and production drops. The small farm is more
Supply
efficient, not only in an economic sense but in a social sense.
A landmark study was done of two California valleys, and this study bears that out. One valley was settled on the basis of small family farms which continue to exist to this day. It supports several small communities. The total output of the area is quite a lot larger than a very similarly blessed valley some 100 miles away that was settled on a corporate structure. The corporations bring in paid workers and when they are finished with them, they send them away. There is very little infrastructure in the area for community activities. There is very little health care and very few educational facilities. The number of families supported is very small and the amount of total economic output does not even begin to compare with that of the other valley which was settled on a family unit basis.
In provinces like my own province of Saskatchewan, our very existence depends on the continuation of relatively modest sized farms that will contribute to the communities and will keep the communities growing and viable economic and social units. The kind of policy the Government seems intent upon pursuing, one of letting the market decide, of pulling away all subsidies, of taking a Margaret Thatcher/Ronald Reagan type economic stance, I contend will decimate not only rural Saskatchewan but all of Saskatchewan. The population of that province has once again been falling for the last three years. As Conservative policies begin to take hold, populations fall. People are leaving because the Government's economic policy has been aimed at supporting very large economic units that do not hire people.
I would also point out that middle-sized agricultural units are, by all studies, virtually as economically efficient as are very large corporate farms. Middle-sized units have the advantage of providing more spin-off jobs and benefits to the surrounding community and provide more overall employment and activity to the whole region, province or country. We think this is the kind of economic policy that should have been proposed during the last election campaign, and we proposed it.
It is notable that in the rural parts of some parts of Canada at least, this proposal was picked up and we are now stronger in rural British Columbia and rural Saskatchewan and are holding our own in rural Ontario. Gradually the message is beginning to be heard and gradually rural Canadians are beginning to see that if they want to continue to be functional, modem communities, ready to go into the 21st century, the kind of policies the New Democrats are advocating for rural Canada are the kind that will include them in the future of Canada. They will not be left out in the hinterland,

Supply
watching metropolitan areas receive the advantages of deregulation, cheaper airfare and relatively cheaper services while they have to pay proportionately increasing costs to stay up to date in our modem world.

I predict that the result will be that some of the provinces
that think they have money or are coming into an election in which the farm vote will matter, will end up boosting coverage levels in their provinces higher than those in surrounding ones. We have seen many examples of that. Recently, Alberta has been paying a so-called pro-benefit to entice the feedlot industiy into that province. It began at some $22 per tonne and had a very predictable effect. It sucked feeder cattle out of Saskatchewan and Manitoba and into Alberta.
When you can get feed grain at $22 a tonne cheaper than the other provinces can, that is a predictable thing for feeders to do. We have also seen the Conservative Government of my own province providing subsidies to cattle feeders trying to keep feeder cattle in Saskatchewan.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would like the Member from MacKenzie (Mr. Althouse) to comment on the impact on the family farm of the high interest rate policy that this Government is pursuing. subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACTOF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, increased interest rates and high interest rates have had a devastating effect on farmers in this country. The debt load has remained for Canada's farms at about $22 billion to $23 billion. The assets that Canadian farmers have to work with have dropped in value during the four years that the $22 billion debt has been in place. As a result, the amount of debt in proportion to assets has been rising compared with the United States whose debt has actually decreased during that period of time. Therefore, we have been left less competitive than before.
If you used that alone as a method of determining whether government payments have been adequate or not, you would have to conclude that they have been inadequate. This is contrary to the recent paper which has come to light from the Department of Agriculture and which argues that perhaps some of these programs are unnecessary. The effect of increasing interest rates also shows up in land values. The Farm Credit Corporation, the Government's own agency, says that in western Canada, particularly in Saskatchewan, land prices have declined over the last four years by more than 38 per cent, largely as a result of increasing interest rates combined with low commodity prices.

Mr. Speaker, the Government talks a lot about the deficit of the country in budgetary terms, but we know that the deficit it is really ashamed of and concerned about is its deficit of ideas, its deficit of a vision, and the deficit of solutions to the challenges facing us today and in the future.
Nothing makes this deficit more evident than how the Government responds to the needs of our post-secondary education system.
I share the concerns expressed by the Canadian Federation of Students and the Canadian Association of University Teachers that stated that the federal Budget
will cut approximately $900 million over the next five years for post-secondary education.
How can the Government block the major artery to Canada's future? If the future of our post-secondary education system were to solely depend on the Government's policy, and if our future as a nation were to depend on the future of our post-secondary education system, then I tell the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) that he may as well cancel tomorrow. I ask the Minister to reconsider his economic policy and allow Canada's youth-

speechtext: The Hon. Member's time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, Sunday, May 28, has been designated AHEPA Day by Archbishop Iakavos of the Greek Orthodox Church of North and South America, and the Bishop of Canada, Bishop Sotirios.
AHEPA stands for the American Hellenic Educational Progressive Association, an organization that plays an important part in the lives of all Canadians and Americans of Greek descent, as well as being active in the civic and philanthropic affairs of Canada.
Since its founding in Canada in 1928, AHEPA programs and activities have helped to strengthen the historical ties which have marked the close relationship between Canada and Greece. AHEPANS have succeeded in combining the best traditions of our two nations whose histories have been marked by dedication to human justice, to freedom, and to our democratic way of life.
AHEPA Day also gives us the opportunity to express the thanks of all Greek Canadians for the privilege and honour of being citizens of our great country Canada.

Mr. Speaker, on May 23, 75 years ago, the S.S. Komagata Maru, carrying 375 Sikh passengers entered the Port of Vancouver. All were

British subjects and had the right to enter Canada but were not allowed to disembark.
Immigration officials used fictitious health problems and processing delays to deny landing rights to the ship. B.C. government officials severed communications to the shore and denied permission to replenish food and water.
After two months of struggle, fear, hunger, thirst and disease, the ship was ordered to leave. On July 23 the Komagata Maru was escorted out of Canadian waters.
My New Democratic colleagues and I consider this to be one of Canada's darkest moments. The unfair and humiliating treatment received by those Sikhs wishing to enter Canada should never have occurred.
By commemorating this past event of racial intolerance, we let Canadian Sikhs know that their suffering has not been forgotten, that we are dedicated to a truly free multicultural Canada where incidents such as this can never again happen, and that this recollection works to ensure that Canada continues to be a better host to all peoples of the world.

Mr. Speaker, the Drummondville Industrial Management Club has held its fourteenth Industrial Olympiad evening event to pay tribute to the manufacturing sector. This is a wonderful opportunity to underline the essential contribution of businesses to our economic and social life. The gold medals went to IBC Enterprises and Venmar Limited and the bronze medals to GTE Sylvania and Multifoam International Products. The silver medallists were Soprema Etancheite and Cascades PSH.
These results stem from the motivation, perseverance, agressiveness and know-how of the region's business people, from their eagerness to take risks in search of excellence and from their reliance on competent employees. It is our duty to emphasize their vital role in the economic growth of our community.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to echo the words of Quebec Government Minister Daniel Johnson who said last Friday that the Conservative Government does not seem to be in any particular hurry to promote the Montreal East economic recovery. Mr. Johnson singled out specific cases, including the Soligaz project for which the Conservative Government still has to honour its promises made during the last election campaign. This project would entail investments of $1 billion and thousands of new jobs in Montreal East. Mr. Johnson also raked the Conservative Government over the coals for failing to give priority to the endorsement of Montreal East funding propositions to upgrade facilities and create jobs. I dare hope the new Minister responsible for the Montreal region will prove to be more efficient than his predecessor.

Mr. Speaker, thousands of Canadian teachers live in fear of lawsuits because the copyright legislation proposed by the former Minister of Communications contained no exemptions for educational purposes.
Teachers must be legally permitted to utilize modem technology to provide current examples for students of various techniques of communication in the media. Easy access to those materials is essential.
Without reasonable exemptions the proposed legislation would revert Canadian classrooms to the era of slate and chalk and make them black holes in the global village.
I urge the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) to provide reasonable exemptions for educators, and to ensure that in the quest for creators' rights the rights of students and educators are not erased.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF PHILIPPINE AMBASSADOR TO CANADA
APPOINTMENT OF PHILIPPINE AMBASSADOR TO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the year 1986 saw the restoration of democracy in the Philippines under President Corazon Aquino, a triumph of the ultimate authority of the Filipino people. The Government of Canada and Canadians of all cultural origins welcomed that event.
Late this morning the Philippine Ambassador to Canada, His Excellency Ramon A. Diaz, presented his credentials to Her Excellency the Governor General of Canada. Mr. Ramon Diaz is a man of high intellect and impeccable integrity. He graduated in law summa cum laude and was chairman of President Aquino's Commission on Good Government. With these credentials, he will prove more than equal to the task of continuing the close, cordial relationship between the Philippines and Canada.
I salute him on his appointment, take pride in welcoming him to Canada, and I hope that Members of the House share my sentiments.

Mr. Speaker, national unity has been a priority of the Government. Recognizing that Atlantic Canada is not only a major pillar in the Confederation of Canada and that its regional and economic isolation places it in a fragile position, I urge the Government to ensure that the vital link, both symbolic and pragmatic-VIA Rail's Atlantic Limited-be left intact.
To that end, I have a petition with more than 1,880 signatures of the residents of Sussex and surrounding area in my riding which I shall be forwarding to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).

Mr. Speaker, when the Government recently announced the closure of bases at Portage la Prairie and Summerside,
residents of Moose Jaw breathed a sigh of relief, thinking that their air base was secure.
However, this may not be the case. In the same manner as the first level of flight training now carried out at CFB Portage will be privatized and moved, so may the second level of flight training CFB at Moose Jaw.
On Friday, May 18, the office of the Associate Minister of Defence admitted that just as Britain has privatized its first and second level of flight training, so may Canada, if the right economic offer comes along. Further, the Government has also admitted that regional job security will not be a factor and training could very easily be conducted elsewhere.
This knowledge, together with the fact that the Government has shown virtually no compassion for the plight of the people in Summerside and Portage la Prairie, will be cold comfort to residents of Moose Jaw.
I call upon the Government to repledge itself to regional economic development and guarantee the residents of Moose Jaw and Portage la Prairie that flight training programs will remain in their present location, regardless of who is conducting the training.
Let the Government finally begin to demonstrate the type of responsibility that the Canadian public expects.

Mr. Speaker, all Canadians are becoming increasingly aware of the economic crisis descending on coastal Atlantic Canada resulting from the downturn in the groundfishery.
Sound measures presently being put in place by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Siddon), together with those already in place, will lead, with adequate enforcement, to a recovery in our fishery over the next three to five years.
However, during the interim, we will need assistance from the Government of Canada. Just as the Government has come to the rescue of communities stricken by agricultural problems in recent years, so do we in Atlantic Canada look for appropriate assistance for families and communities dependent upon the Atlantic fishery for their livelihood. Such special measures should be taken not only to assist fishermen, but also plant
May 23, 1989

workers and operators, boat builders, and boat yard workers.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring to the attention of the House a matter of great urgency and concern both to Nova Scotians and to all Canadians.
Two legal education pamphlets have been distributed in Nova Scotia. One is bigoted and racially discriminatory. The first pamphlet entitled "Criminal Law" has a picture of three black children on the cover. The second pamphlet entitled "The Young Offenders Act and You" has a picture of a white boy. The three black children on the first pamphlet are not criminals, and their families did not give permission for their children's pictures to be used.
I find it disconcerting to think that someone would put the picture of three black children on a pamphlet entitled "Criminal Law", without portraying a group of children of various racial backgrounds.
In light of the fact that those pamphlets were produced with funding assistance from the federal Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) and as a joint project of the Public Legal Education Organizations of the Atlantic Provinces, I expect an apology not only from the head of this organization, but also from the Attorney General of Nova Scotia and, more important, the federal Solicitor General. I also expect these pamphlets to be pulled immediately, and this contemptible situation must never be allowed to happen again.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR RENEWAL OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
REQUEST FOR RENEWAL OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the federal-provincial forestry development agreements are about to expire. These are five-year cooperation agreements to meet the forestry needs of each province. The agreements now in place provide total funding of approximately $1.1 billion over their lifetime: $571 million from the federal Government and $520 million from the provincial level.
Mr. Speaker, as a Member of Parliament for a forestry region, I ask the Government of Canada to renew these federal-provincial agreements because they really have an impact on forestry development. Renewing these agreements is essential to the continued development of Canada's forests, so as to reach publicly supported environmental objectives and to maintain their important contribution to the regional and national economy.

Mr. Speaker, on May 20, it was reported that the federal Government has quietly implemented a new policy of allowing government advertising to go to agencies not fully owned by Canadians because existing Canadian agencies have been purchased by Americans.
On May 9, the Minister responsible for government advertising appeared before the Consumer and Corporate Affairs Committee and said that his Department uses only Canadian owned agencies, even if that meant excluding some 20 of the largest 25 agencies in this country because they are foreign owned.
At that time did not the Minister know that his Department was in the process of changing its policies to

May 23, 1989
conform with the terms of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade deal? If so, why did he not tell the committee that he knew what was going on in his Department and that the policy was being changed?
Government advertising worth millions of dollars every year is awarded without tender. The Minister must stick to his statement in the committee and instruct his officials that only Canadian agencies can advertise for the Canadian Government.

subtopic: FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, May 23, 1989 marks the fortieth anniversary of the Federal Republic of Germany.
Since 1949, the Federal Republic has experienced dramatic economic reconstruction and has become one of the leading industrial nations of the world.
Canada's cordial relations with West Germany flow from our collective defence of western values of democracy and freedom as part of the NATO Alliance.
Of the thousands of United Empire Loyalists who came to Canada following the American Revolution, a significant number were of German origin. Together with Mennonites from Pennsylvania who settled in Waterloo County, these German speaking people founded the City of Berlin, now known as Kitchener. Today, Canadians whose mother tongue is German comprise Canada's third largest ethnic group.
I invite all Members of Parliament to join with me and the constituents of Kitchener in extending our congratulations on this fortieth anniversary and in expressing our hope for continued good relations and prosperity between our two nations.

Mr. Speaker, the Government's Budget is devastating to agriculture. Some farm organizations estimate this Budget will cost an individual farmer up to $2,000. Even the Government's own officials say that it is at least between $700 and $1,000. No other sector in this economy has been hit so hard or asked to give so much.
Many farmers in Haldimand-Norfolk are living from milk pay cheque to milk pay cheque. It is time the Government woke up and realized that agriculture is the foundation of our economy. Our agriculture industry is very complex. Does it not realize that success in food production is based on long-term planning? Without warning it has taken away the programs our farmers have planned around, have been counting on, and set them adrift with nothing to take their place.
I suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) that his Budget will do irreparable damage to our agriculture industry. It is just one more step in the many his Government has taken which will inevitable increase our dependency on the United States, this time for our food supply. These actions are irresponsible and unacceptable and I ask the Government-
