subtopic: CAPITAL GAINS EXEMPTION ON FAMILY FARM
CAPITAL GAINS EXEMPTION ON FAMILY FARM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, until recently members of the NDP were telling farmers that their policy of taxing 100 per cent of all capital gains would not apply to the family farm. We now learn that this policy has its limitations.
To quote the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Cowichan (Mr. Stupich) on May 11:
The party position is that if the farm is staying within the family and is being passed down in the form of an inheritance or a transfer, then there should be no tax at all, at least not on the first half million. However, if it is being sold to someone else, then why should it not be like any other asset of industry or business?
It should not be treated like any other asset of industry because the farm is the farmer's pension plan and because the capital gains exemption rewards farmers for their years of sacrifice, risk, and labour.
The NDP wants to bring farmers back to the capital gains rules that existed before the introduction of the $500,000 exemption in May 1985. That is simply not acceptable to this side.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC AGREEMENT
JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1975, the Grand Council of Crees won an important recognition of their role, status, and culture in the form of the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement.
The federal Government's responsibilities include the protection of health and the environment. The Government has done very little to live up to its part of the agreement. The lakes behind the dams are contaminated with mercury, depriving the Cree of fish on which they depend for their livelihood.
The Minister responsible, in his 1988 annual report on the agreement, ignores the mercury problem. Now we learn that the administration of the agreement has been assigned to the federal environmental assessment and review office, adding a new work-load to an already overburdened staff.
We urge the Government to discharge its responsibilities to the Grand Council of Cree by providing the administrator with the funds needed to do the job. The James Bay Agreement cannot and should not be treated lightly by the Government.

Mr. Speaker, my questions about human rights are directed to the Acting Prime Minister.
The ARMX show which is currently taking place has grown over the years from a show intended to supply Canada's defence needs to a show promoting the international trade of military equipment. Representatives of countries which routinely violate human rights meet with international arms suppliers.
This is not the international tulip show that we have here in Ottawa, or an international auto show; it is an international arms show.
Oral Questions
If ARMX is supposedly an exhibit to provide equipment to Canada's military, why are representatives from countries which violate human rights attending this display? Why are representatives from countries which are not our allies attending this international arms bazaar? What is the role of non-NATO countries at this exhibit?
speakername: Right Hon. John N. Timer@Leader of the Opposition

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we had the debate on ARMX in the House on Friday. I would like to assure the Leader of the Opposition once again that ARMX is a trade show. I was there this morning. It provides an opportunity for companies to display and provide goods and services which are used by our Department.
The participants with the displays are members of NATO countries. Of course, there are many Canadian companies as well, and many companies from British Columbia. I am sure the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition would enjoy an opportunity of visiting those displays.
It is organized by a private sector company, and the private sector company has advised us that it had sent invitations to members of the diplomatic community, to the military attaches, to certain members of that community. It also sent an information letter to the various embassies in Ottawa.
But the purpose of the exhibition is to provide the information about potential goods and services to be supplied to the Canadian Armed Forces to ensure that we can operate as cost effectively and efficiently as possible.

The Minister says this is sponsored by a private sector outfit, but she was there this morning on behalf of the Department of National Defence, supposedly, and this outfit would not exist without sponsorship from that Department.

Mr. Speaker, Canada is acting as a shopping centre for arms for human rights violators.
Last week the Secretary of State for External Affairs made an non-credible statement to the House of Commons Committee on External Affairs. He said: "Your question was specifically about South African participation in this private event. If they are there, they have a right to be there".

May 23, 1989

As far as he is concerned, South Africa can use Canada as a venue for making arms deals. Why will the Government not tell Canada who has been invited, and under whose auspices they are there at this international arms bazaar?
Is Iran there? Is Panama there? Is Chile there? Is El Salvador there? Will the Minister produce a list of participants?

Let me assure my colleague that ARMX is not an arms bazaar.

If he would go for himself he would find that out. He would find out that there are companies such as Mesotech from British Columbia-

subtopic: DENUNCIATION OF ABUSE COMMITTED BY CERTAIN MEMBER COUNTRIES OF FRANCOPHONIE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
DENUNCIATION OF ABUSE COMMITTED BY CERTAIN MEMBER COUNTRIES OF FRANCOPHONIE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government is reducing foreign aid but encouraging international arms sales to countries that violate human rights. The Government pretends to respect human rights as long as they do not call into question the Government's commercial interests or diplomatic relations. I therefore ask the Minister or the acting External Affairs Minister why the Government has not announced in advance that it intends to denounce vigorously the human rights abuses of some Francophone countries at the Francophone Summit now being held in Senegal.
speakername: Right Hon. John N. Dimer@Leader of the Opposition

subtopic: DENUNCIATION OF ABUSE COMMITTED BY CERTAIN MEMBER COUNTRIES OF FRANCOPHONIE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that the Secretary of State (for External Affairs) has indeed placed a resolution for debate at the Dakar conference. I believe and hope that this will be a beginning of the improvement he desires.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN OVERFISHING OFF COAST OF NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. As he will know, foreign overfishing off Newfoundland's coast has reached crisis proportions. For example, in 1986 the European Community which had been assigned a catch quota of 19,000 tonnes by NAFO actually caught 110,000 tonnes.
Did the Prime Minister in his Friday meeting with Francois Mitterrand enlist the support of the French President to beat some sense into the European Community, including France, to get them to stop the wilful destruction of our fish stock before 100,000 fishermen and plant workers in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia see their livelihoods disappear forever?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International D-ade):
subsubtopic: FOREIGN OVERFISHING OFF COAST OF NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this serious problem that we have experienced since 1986 with reference to overfishing on the nose and tail of the Grand Banks is a matter the

Government is addressing and has addressed now and ever since it started to occur.
However, if my hon. friend wants to ask the questions in this manner, the fact remains that his own Government gave 9,500 tonnes of northern cod every year for a period of five years to the European Community. It was not forced to do that. It was a voluntary action it took. That was in excess of 45,000 tonnes of northern cod. That was inside the Canadian 200-mile limit of which 1,575 tonnes went to France.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN OVERFISHING OFF COAST OF NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext: When was that?

subsubtopic: FOREIGN OVERFISHING OFF COAST OF NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext: These were the years, Mr. Speaker, from 1983 to 1987, if the Hon. Member opposite wants the years.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN OVERFISHING OFF COAST OF NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext: Were you not in power then?

subsubtopic: FOREIGN OVERFISHING OFF COAST OF NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
With respect to President Mitterrand, the Government is pursuing this issue with all members of the European Community.
On June 2, I will be pursuing this issue with Mr. Andriessen who is the Commissioner for External Affairs of the European Community. We hope to persuade the European Community to be conscious of the need for conservation and proper care of the environment with respect to fish, as well as with respect to everything that pertains to the environment.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister talks about a gift. He will know of course that it was a trade-off which had the effect of preventing overfishing. Why does he not tiy something that would prevent overfishing?
The announcement of the cabinet committee on the fishery on Friday I suggest pandered more to Mitterrand's presence here in Ottawa than it did to Newfoundland's need and vital interest in the matter. Does that committee have the mandate to recommend economic sanctions against those international bandits who are out there thumbing their noses at NAFO and Canada? Will the committee consider extending our fisheries jurisdiction to the nose and tail of the Grand Banks to give functional control to Canada over these transboundary stock?
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's use of this type of language does not help in this issue.

Oh, oh!
Oral Questions

The European Community and other nations are fishing in international waters outside the 200-mile economic limit recognized by most countries of the world and within which Canada has some control. To use this type of language with respect to those who fish there is not helpful.
Canada is not the world's policeman for areas outside the 200-mile limit. What we are attempting to do is to persuade the countries that fish into the northwest Atlantic that they are spoiling the fishery for themselves as well as for others. We are going to attempt to pursue whatever rights we have as a coastal state with respect to straddling stocks that cross to and from the 200-mile limit.
A unilateral extension of boundaries was not attempted by our predecessors. All they did was give fish to the European Community. I do not think it will serve us well to try the same on it again.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Associate Minister of National Defence.
A Chilean colonel was window-shopping this morning at the ARMX military flea market, a shopping opportunity to which South Africa had been invited as well. The Government denies any arms sales were concluded with governments with a reputation for failing to respect human rights, despite the fact that these countries were represented.
If the Government has nothing to hide, why doesn't it publish a list of all transactions involving strategic military equipment with countries that do not respect human rights?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I could once again try to explain the purpose of ARMX, it is to provide a forum in which companies that provide goods and services to the Canadian Armed Forces can come together to provide this opportunity and display. Many of the people in our Department who are responsible for procurement attend ARMX to see the latest in training, the latest in

Oral Questions
simulation, and the latest kinds of weapon systems that are available.
The purpose of ARMX is not to provide a forum for the sale or information about weapons to Third World countries.
As the Hon. Member knows, we have a policy through the Department of External Affairs which limits the sale of military weapons to any countries with human rights violations.

Mr. Speaker, we all go window shopping to watch other people buy things.
If there is this policy that prohibits the sale of arms to countries which abuse human rights, then surely the Government ought to be able to come clean and tell the people of Canada and Parliament just what arms are sold to what countries that are noted for abusing rights.
Why does the Government not come clean? It is a simple thing. If it is honestly pursuing a policy of an embargo of arms shipments to human rights abusers, then tell us what is being sold.
Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International
Trade): Mr. Speaker-
Oh, oh!
Bail her out, John.

speechtext: The Hon. Minister.

Mr. Speaker, the policy with respect to the export of arms from Canada has been explained by the Secretary of State for External Affairs on many occasions. We closely control the export of military goods. We do not export military goods to countries which pose a threat to Canada or its allies. We do not export goods to those countries involved in or under imminent threat of hostilities, or countries under UN Security Council sanctions, or to countries whose governments have a persistent record of serious violations of the human rights of their citizens. That policy is administered by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. There has never been a person in that position who has been more scrupulous and more attentive in that direction than the Secretary of State for External Affairs. We have nothing to apologize for.
Hear, hear!

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STUDY OF SALES OF GOODS FOR MILITARY USE
REQUEST FOR STUDY OF SALES OF GOODS FOR MILITARY USE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs is also a great advocate of freedom of information. There were many who witnessed a Chilean colonel window shopping at Lansdowne Park who would bring Canadian policy into serious question. I would ask the Government this: why will it not make the list available, if necessary to a special all-Party parliamentary task force, to study all aspects of sales of all goods that could be used for military use? I would ask the Government also to support a United Nations initiative for an arms trade register. What does he answer to that?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STUDY OF SALES OF GOODS FOR MILITARY USE

Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman is a victim of controlled hysteria. Canada closely controls the exports of all military goods. The total exports in 1987 were $1.8 billion, of which 71 per cent went to the United States of America. A further 19 per cent went to other NATO countries. Only 10 per cent was exported to non-NATO countries. That was very, very carefully controlled.
Are the hon. gentlemen saying that they do not want a military or defence industry in this country? Do they want to do away with the tens of thousands of jobs that are involved?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Hon. Member's question. She raises a very important point about economic considerations for the Atlantic region, and particularly as it relates to the fish stocks. That is a very important and urgent matter that has to be dealt with. Of course, Cabinet will be looking at it and taking whatever steps necessary to ensure that the fishermen and industry in the Atlantic region can in fact adjust to this difficult issue. We will be looking at exploring various options, plus taking a very strong stand internationally in terms of dealing with the issue of over-fishing, as my colleague, the Minister for International Trade, has alluded to.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. I would just tell the Deputy Prime Minister that I certainly understand the need for defending our Atlantic coast, as we have always done on the East Coast.
Hear, hear!

You cannot hit anybody on this side on your defence closures because I think they were ridiculous. However, Mr. Speaker, the Minister did not answer. We had one Minister on the weekend saying a committee was set up. We had Premier John Buchanan in Nova Scotia saying that he welcomed the Prime Minister's order to set up a committee to take an "in depth look at the problem of Atlantic Canadians associated with many things, including the federal Budget."

Just before we closed for the luncheon recess, the Member for Durham (Mr. Stevenson) asked me two or three questions which I would like to respond to quickly. First, he asked if the program that I outlined on behalf of the New Democratic Party for agricultural support was a program like the Common Agricultural Policy in the European community. It is not. If it is modelled after any program, it is probably closest to the United States. What we did was divide the amount of production that is produced within the country and decided that we could provide some price guarantees for the production that is in fact consumed within the country. Initially we said we would set the price guarantees equivalent to the guarantees established south of the line, that eventually we would move to cost of production based on costs for the medium-sized farm. The Hon. Member for Durham asked what type of economic impact our program would have in comparison to the programs that have been brought in ad hoc by the Government. They would have
May 23, 1989

less economic impact to the extent that the programs that were introduced by the Government were aimed at farms much larger than the median size. I would remind Members of the House that the median size is where half the farms are larger and half the farms are smaller. By targeting that size, there would be virtually a neutral economic impact. Rather than focusing less dollars on the average and smaller-sized farm, which our program would do, the Government's approach has been to encourage largeness only for the sake of maximizing the amount of subsidies that the Government has tended to make available. Our program would not provide that type of counter-incentive to the system. It would be virtually program-neutral, and would have permitted economic forces to make the decision as to whether or not a farm should be larger. That decision would not be subject to doing it in order to maximize the amount of government subsidies that would be available.

It would be very interesting to know exactly what was meant in the memorandum of April 17 where it stated that the increased risk is real and a change in policy is called for as a result of the Government's announcement on April 14 by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Mazankowski).
I hope that the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of State for Agriculture will come clean and clarify the exact status of the supply management industry across Canada, especially as it affects the dairy industry. There are similar concerns being expressed by poultry, egg, and turkey producers who are also under national farm marketing regimes.
It seems to me that as the Official Opposition put this motion today, we are seeing a country whose agriculture industry is facing perhaps the most uncertain time in history. It is not only the uncertainty of what is happening at the GATT or with the free trade deal, but also the uncertainty as a result of broken promises. There was an ironclad commitment made last fall during the election campaign that marketing boards would be preserved, that they were safe, and nothing was going to happen to them. Yet, we see what has already happened. Banks are withdrawing their credit support. In the first few months of this year marketing boards have lost their ability to raise prices where input costs rise. There is great concern about what is happening.
This weekend there was a report in the Ottawa Citizen about a young couple who farm in Manitoba. In the article Nancy Drul was quoted as stating:
"It's hot, it's dry, it's windy, and they're broke. This is a very scary situation."
The article further states:
Farmers like the Druls were stunned this spring when, in the course of one week, they watched the federal government cut and slash at programs that carried many through the tough times of the late 1980s.
In that black week of late April, the government:
Reduced the subsidy it pays for hauling grain to ports;
Said there would be no interim payment from the Western Grains Stabilization Fund. (Last year farmers received $695 million);
Announced initial prices farmers are paid for wheat and barley at the elevator will decrease;
And introduced a budget that will remove some interest-free cash
advances to fanners and, next year, remove a fuel-tax rebate farmers
have received.
The family points out that last year they had $100,000 in revenues and $68,000 in costs. They point out that one-quarter of the revenue came from Government payments and that most of that will be gone in this crop year. There is extreme hardship and extreme concern out there.
The food processing industry across the country is saying that the Government must make up its mind about marketing boards within one year. We expected that if the Tories won the election and implemented the free trade deal, with its commitment to the Americans which considered farm marketing boards to be subsidies, that the removal of subsidies would take several years. Now we see the grocery products manufacturing industry saying that there will be chaos in one year unless the Government caves in and gets rid of the marketing boards. There is extreme concern about exactly what will happen and what is the Government agenda.
Nothing has destroyed dreams more than the Government's Budget, with the elimination of credit by banks to those under supply management systems, as well as reduced interest rate support.
I want to refer to a group that usually supports the Government. The Western Canadian Wheat Growers point out that since April, 1988, the Bank of Canada's prime rate has climbed from 9.6 per cent to 12.6 per cent, resulting in a potential drain of more than $350 million from the western farm economy. They state that the second blow hits when farmers take their crops to market because high interest rates artificially deflate the value of the Canadian dollar, resulting in lower grain receipts on international markets. They say western Canadian farmers cannot absorb this two-way cash squeeze.
If that is what the Government's friends are saying about it, one can imagine what those who are less enchanted by the Tories are saying. They are in complete disarray as to how they will cope.
I believe that the Agriculture Committee of the House did a monumental piece of work last year in looking at one of the most important aspects of agriculture, the cost of financing. We worked for several months on a report
May 23, 1989

entitled "The $22 Billion Problem", which pointed out that some $6 billion worth of funding could not be adequately serviced. Since then, interest rates have risen dramatically.
The Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek- Assiniboia, the Member for Mackenzie (Mr. Althouse) and other Members in the House who served on that committee looked to the Speech from the Throne with great interest.
There were three lines about agriculture in the Speech from the Throne. One statement was that the whole agriculture situation was too much of a drain on the economy of the country.
There were a number of recommendations in our report on innovative ways to finance agriculture, especially for new farmers. Not one of those recommendations was implemented in the Budget. In fact, the Budget is designed to add some $500 million in extra costs to farmers over two years. Crop insurance is being cut back by $200 million. The transportation program is being cut back by $60 million. The rail branch line rehabilitation program is being cut back by $48 million. All of these programs were promises made by the Government.
Others include the dairy export program which is cut by $12 million; the Canadian Dairy Commission which is cut by $10 million, the commodity based loan program which is cut by $15 million.
The grain and crop advance payments program will be cut by $54 million over two years.
There are two main subsidized interest rate programs. One is the crop advance payment program under which the Government provides some financial interest rate support so that farmers do not have to sell their crop immediately in the fall but can hold it until the price is better or transportation and other factors are right in order to get maximum benefit. That program is being cut in direct violation of a campaign commitment in 1984.
The other subsidized interest rate program is the commodity based mortgage. While I was not entirely in favour of this program, the Government fully supported it. In some instances it did provide lower interest rates,
Supply
although the farmer would have had to pay more if the commodity value rose. That program was also cut.
When one considers these measures, we can see that farmers will face much greater difficulty than they have in the past, at least as far as interest rates are concerned.
It is also interesting to look at the Budget itself to see how many of the cut-backs listed therein were listed as subsidies in the free trade deal. It will be interesting to find out from the Minister the results of his meeting today with Mr. Yeutter to see how many of the subsidies in the United States that are listed in this agreement have been cut out.
The cut-backs in the Budget include agricultural stabilization, the At and East transportation subsidy, ARDA, the Prairie Branchline Rehabilitation Program and the Farm Credit Corporation Commodity Based Mortgage.
While the domestic price gap of the Canadian Wheat Board will not be removed, clearly the Government is indicating that it wants to get rid of the Canadian Wheat Board. It has already removed oats, and it will be interesting to see if Mr. Yeutter is putting the pressure on the Minister today to remove barley.
While it is clear that the Government is attempting to remove most of these subsidies, I do not understand why it would do so. It was my belief that the Government would negotiate with the Americans over the next five to seven years a code of subsidies that would not be subject to countervail or dumping, as well as negotiate an arbitration procedure when disputes occur.
However, the domestic price of wheat has been removed and at least six or maybe more of the subsidies outlined in this agreement have already been given away. As far as agriculture is concerned, all the subsidies will be removed before the negotiations. I only hope the Americans are doing the same thing as the Toiy Government. There will be little to negotiate with regard to an agricultural subsidies code because most of these subsidies are being wiped out unilaterally.
Usually you get something when you give something when negotiating. According to this procedure, the Government is unilaterally cancelling most of the items which are identified as subsidies. I read with great interest the Minister's speech which he gave in Toronto

May 23, 1989
Supply
at the National Agrimarketing Association Conference. The Minister said in his speech:
The trade agreement provides for a dispute settlement mechanism that will overcome irritants and help enhance market access. It's going to ensure anti-dumping and countervail actions are applied fairly.
I thought that that was very interesting. Then he went on to state: "The law, not political self-interest, will govern the trade process."
It is very interesting that a couple of weeks ago the United States slapped a countervail duty on our pork going into the United States. I could not believe the Minister's words. It seems to me that if there ever was political self-interest, the fact that the United States is to impose countervail duty on pork is it. The reason the Americans were able to do it is because after the trade deal was passed last October the Omnibus Trade Bill was brought into the United States Senate. Senator Bachus proposed an amendment stating that a countervail when applied to a primary product could be applied equally to a secondary phase of that product. You will recall, Madam Speaker, that in 1936 the United States imposed a countervail duty on our hogs going into the United States. Immediately that amendment was passed in the Omnibus Trade Bill to the countervail duty law, the United States pork producers petitioned the International Trade Commission for a countervail. It is being applied on an interim basis.
I really do not think that the Minister was thinking about the application of that countervail duty on our pork when he made this speech in Toronto in which he talked about the beauties of the situation, since our pork producers are already facing extremely low prices. Now there is a countervail duty as well.
In the same speech given to the National Agrimarketing Association conference the Minister talked about the quality of our beef products going into the United States. If there has ever been concern expressed it is with respect to what is happening in terms of our grading standards in beef. What is happening is that we are not harmonizing through negotiations with the United States, but the United States is shipping larger quantities of no-rolle or ungraded beef into Canada. Our producers are having to compete with that. Our whole grading system, which is one of the best in the world, is being
destroyed. That is regrettable. If we require beef produced in this country which is going into interprovincial trade to be graded then the same should apply to beef coming into Canada from the United States.
I have set out a number of our concerns. Our agriculture industry is facing extremely difficult times and great uncertainty. This is seen when one talks to western farmers who are not sure whether the Government will come through on its payment for drought assistance since in the Estimates there was only half enough money to pay for it. We do not know whether or not the Canadian Wheat Board will be destroyed because of pressure from the United States. The Government has already knuckled under and taken oats out from under its control.
I believe we are facing a very difficult time and great uncertainty. At the same time we are facing this great uncertainty, the Government seems to be withdrawing all types of programs not only to assist the Minister of Finance but to implement the free trade deal.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACT OF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to direct a question to my hon. friend from Algoma. He made reference to the $22 billion problem, the report rendered last year by the Standing Committee on Agriculture. Indeed, he was generous enough to refer to it as a monumental piece of work. Perhaps he was overly generous in his description of it.
What I recall in particular about the hearings that went on before the report was written and in the preparation of the report was that there were really no quick fixes, no easy solutions out there. All of them would involve taxpayers' money. I think there has been perhaps a universal desire to see lower long-term interest rates for the agriculture community. However, I want to ask my friend what criteria he would propose be set out for such a program if indeed he favours one. How would it be paid for?
During the course of those hearings on farm debt we heard over and over again from various responsible farm groups that imposing an artificially low interest rate in agriculture really did not do anyone any favours because the interest rate concession inevitably becomes capitalized into higher asset values, higher land and machinery prices and, in effect, exacerbates the problem. It does
May 23, 1989

not really help the young fanner. It does not do anything for him.
It seems to me the key is not to seek special concessions for one sector but rather to try to get interest rates down across the board in the country.
Does my hon. friend agree with that? Or does he adhere to the idea that there should be special interest rates for the farm community? If so, how would he structure them? How would he propose to pay for them?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACT OF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member raises two very interesting points. Clearly, there are a number of programs to which he agreed when our committee reported. I will not try to go into the details of that half-inch thick document.
Interest rates in the country are very high. We are about 3.5 points above the United States, as I understand the rates right now. That imposes a great cost on Canadian producers. Mr. Harvey McEwen, the President of the Western Canadian Wheat Growers, has pointed out that the increase in interest rates by almost 3.5 per cent in the last year is costing western Canadian agriculture some $350 million per year. That is a great cost to our producers. It is something that is set by the Government. Whether or not it is an under the table deal by the Government of Canada as part of the free trade deal, we do not know. Certainly, when Congressmen, Members of Parliament and Senators meet all the talk is about the veiy low exchange rate by the United States officials. Whether there is a deal between the Government of Canada and the United States to keep our interest rates 3.5 per cent to 4 per cent above the United States, nobody knows for sure.
The Government does not have many programs. It is not wise enough to choose some of the programs such as the shared appreciation mortgage program, the stabilization fund, or some other of the programs which the Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek-Assiniboia (Mr. Wilson) and other members of the committee recommended. As a matter of fact, the Government did not do anything. It did not provide any assistance even though as Harvey McEwen said in the letter he sent to every Member of Parliament, interest costs have gone up by $350 million in western Canada alone. I am sure if
Supply
that is applied right across the country we are probably looking at $700 million or $800 million.
The Government brought in the commodity based mortgage which, as far as I know, is the only subsidized program around. It even cut that out. It was not a very large program but the Hon. Member and others have said that it was very good. It involved some $15 million over a several year period. Even that was cut out.
It seems to me that programs like the Advance Payment Program really gets the farmer two ways. Not only does he not have that support to market at a more convenient time or a time when he can get his best price, but it tends to push everybody, especially those who are in a financially hard-pressed position, to market as soon as the crop comes off. That only exacerbates the situation and drives prices lower. The net value of that program is probably way above the cost, which I think is $27 million a year. We have the crop being marketed over a period of time, rather than everybody, especially those who are in a difficult financial position, marketing as soon as the crop comes off.
I hope I have been able to clarify these important matters for the Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek-Assiniboia.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACT OF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, may I say I appreciate clarifying the matters earlier, and I certainly appreciate your advice.
I would like to participate in this debate from the perspective of a prairie Member of Parliament. My riding of Swift Current-Maple Creek-Assiniboia contains some 23,000 square miles of farming and ranching area, across more than half of southern Saskatchewan. My riding would be more dependent or certainly as dependent on the prosperity of the agricultural sector, especially the grain sector, as any constituency in the nation.
This opposition day motion purports to criticize this Government for its actions toward agriculture. I must say at the outset, I am rather surprised that the opposition Members would pick a topic like this. I recall they did so a couple of years ago and the debate went on for several days around the clock. It was a most successful opportu-

May 23, 1989
Supply
nity for Members on this side to be able to outline and explain the enormous response which our Government has made to Canadian agriculture during its term of office.
During the 1986 Throne Speech, the statement was made that the Government would spare no effort in protecting the interests of the Canadian farmer. I suggest that that sums up the policy upon which our Government has embarked.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Mazankowski), and the Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds) (Mr. Mayer), have consistently pursued that policy in support of Canadian producers. They have done it in two ways: externally, through negotiations, seeking order in agricultural trade. They have done it through the Cairns group, the group of grain exporting nations. They have done so through the latest multinational round of GATT. They will continue to pursue that elusive goal of trying to bring order to agricultural trade world-wide to try to reduce and ultimately bring an end to a disastrous round of production and export subsidies which have been so harmful and destructive to grain prices internationally, and which have so seriously affected our grain producers.
Domestically, the policy has manifested itself in a number of programs which Members in this House, and certainly those in the farm community, will be very familiar with. This Government has cushioned farmers hurt by those external problems that I mentioned, the external trade wars, as well as the drought problems here at home. There have been a whole series of programs, amendments to Western Grain Stabilization, improvements to crop insurance. There was a 1985 drought program. There was the Canada Special Grains Programs, 1 and 2, which contributed respectively $1 billion and $1.1 billion to Canadian farmers in order to overcome the hurt that was inflicted on them as a result of the the grain war between the European Economic Community and the United States. Last year we had the drought problem. This was not just in Saskatchewan but across many parts of Canada.
I want to briefly address the grain sector, the impact of the drought, and perhaps make some comments in
regard to the Canadian Wheat Board. Certainly those are areas which impact strongly on the Prairies and western Canada generally.
My Province of Saskatchewan is one which is very dependent on grain export dollars. Regardless of the much needed diversification that is taking place across Saskatchewan and western Canada, there seems to be little question but that agriculture will continue to be the force that shapes the prairie economy.
Against a backdrop of historically low grain prices occasioned by trade wars beyond our borders and of poor yields occasioned by weather related disasters which are beyond the purview of Government, it is remarkable that the Province of Saskatchewan, so dependent on agriculture and especially the grain export sector, has been able to virtually maintain its population. It has been able to survive the most difficult times certainly since the 1930s. I suggest it is because the ravages of low prices and drought have been in large measure cushioned by a number of federal and federal-provincial programs which were designed to ameliorate the situation, indeed programs which were unprecedented in their magnitude.
I would like to make a few remarks relating specifically to the 1988 drought. I believe that that is in part the subject matter of the Opposition motion that is before us today. The federal Government has proved its commitment to the agricultural industry since it was elected in 1984. The help given to producers hurt by the 1988 drought is no exception.
The Government announced in May, 1988 a $12 million program to assist in water development. That was over and above regular moneys that were allotted to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Administration. This $12 million was to help producers to develop water supplies. The program was an enormous success. Indeed, I am told it has been over-subscribed. In June, there was another $153 million program announced to assist western livestock producers who were hit by a drought. There were payments of up to $60 per head.
In addition, there was the green feed program to help alleviate a feed shortage. For the first time ever a there was tax deferral on the forced sale of livestock. This is something that The Cattlemen's Association and western cattle producers have requested over several genera-

tions, and it seemed eminently reasonable, and I am happy to say that our Government was able to respond.
Last fall, the Canadian Crop Drought Assistance Program was announced. This is a program that would provide approximately $850 million to producers who suffered crop damage because of the drought. As the impact of the drought started to affect cereal crops last summer, the Government focused its efforts on finding solutions to the problem. There were discussions with federal-provincial drought committees. Producers were heard at meetings in Guelph and in Saskatoon last August. There were some things that emerged from those meetings. There was agreement, I believe, that any assistance should compliment the existing crop insurance programs and the integrity of these programs should be maintained. The integrity of crop insurance was preserved and will continue to be maintained. Crop insurance is, after all, the producers first line of defence against disaster. Crop insurance works well.
As a result of the 1988 drought, crop insurance paid out a record $900 million. It is clear that crop insurance can be improved. There is work ongoing at the present time between the federal and provincial Governments, and with the input of farm organizations toward trying to make some meaningful and useful changes to make crop insurance more responsive to the needs of producers. In the summer and fall of 1988 the extent of the damage was great. It was beyond what the existing safety net of crop insurance and stabilization was able to cope. Some crop insurance prices reflected depressed prices which were brought on by the U.S.-common market trade war, so producers needed better protection. With the assistance of producers the four cornerstones of the Canadian Crop Drought Assistance Program were set.
First, the program had to be national in nature. Second, it should apply equally to all commodities. Third, the program had to be targeted because there were certain portions of five provinces where there was drought and where producers were affected.
Finally, the program should be crop specific. The drought program was designed to provide the most assistance to those who were hurt the most and there has been extensive research and data collection required to accomplish that goal.
Supply
The Government consulted farm organizations which told the Government that drought assistance should be targeted very carefully in order to reach those farmers who were hit hardest. Statistics have been obtained from provincial crop insurance offices in order to obtain crop information on areas right down to the township level.
This program covers five provinces, more than 100 different crops from wheat to apples. More than 4,500 townships have been designated as drought areas. I would like to outline how the program works. It was recognized that farmers in the most severe drought areas would need assistance quickly to help them put in a crop this year.
Provincial crop insurance figures were used to designate three types of drought areas; severe, moderate and least affected. These areas were preliminary and were designed to show where interim payments would be made and for those purposes only. Further areas could be eligible for assistance later when final provincial crop insurance figures become available. Interim flat acreage payments were directed at farmers who were in the designated areas initially identified as severe or moderate. Final payments will be made, according to the officials, in July to all eligible producers.
The payment formula will target the assistance to those areas which were hardest hit. The assistance payments are, of course, in addition to crop insurance. All grains, oil seeds, special crops, vegetables and fruits produced in drought areas are eligible for assistance. Producer review committees have been established in each of the provinces to handle appeals under the program.
The program is on track. To date, interim payments have been processed, cheques valued at over $211 million have been mailed out to over 56,000 producers. More than 121,000 applications were mailed directly to producers and over 114,000 completed applications have been returned to the drought program administration.
A process is being put in place to handle requests from producers whose areas may not initially have been designated for assistance. The fact is that in regard to this program the Government is keeping its commitments, is living up to its promises, as it has every step of the way over the preceding four years.

May 23, 1989
Supply
The drought presented problems to producers that are as varied as the crops produced across this country. The drought program, if it is to be successful, has to recognize the complexities and it must deliver assistance accordingly.
The final program calculations will be completed when the provinces provide us with final data. This data will allow the administrators of the program to provide yield and price coverage above what has already been provided by crop insurance.
The federal Government recognized the need to get as much money as possible to producers without the benefit of the final yield data from the crop insurance offices. To that end application forms were mailed out to producers on the basis of the data provided to the administrators of the program by the provincial crop insurance agencies. On the basis of this data forwarded in late January, interim payments were made. These payments were as high as possible without risking over-payment.
The program was built on cornerstones of being a national program, of being crop specific, and being targeted to those who need help the most. It is very easy to criticize a program like this because we all know from past experience that any program which is a substitute for the market-place involves the designation of some artificial criteria. You have to start drawing lines on maps. Whenever you do that some people feel good because they are on the right side and other people feel badly because they are on the wrong side. It does not matter because you can erase the line and move it, but, there will still be an equal number of people who feel aggrieved. So, no one is suggesting that this is a substitute for the workings of the market-place. What we are saying is that it is an attempt on the part of the federal Government to redress the problems which arose as a result of that unfortunate 1988 drought.
If we contrast this program with the Special Grains Programs of the previous couple of years, it is easy to see why it does take some time. The Special Grains Programs were designed to address the price shortfall occasioned by the shoot out in the trade war between the Europeans and the Americans.
Moneys were paid to all producers on the basis of prices having been affected as a result of the trade war. It was a universal program. All producers in the country qualified.
This particular Crop Drought Assistance Program is infinitely more complex and complicated because it attempts to target those producers who are in the affected drought areas and then it goes beyond that to a further degree of fine tuning and attempts to gauge the amount of assistance to the severity of the crop damage suffered by the producer. This is an enormously complex task and if nothing else, it points out the need for reform of the basic programs.
We are trying to strengthen the farm income safety net so that hopefully, in the future, it will be possible to get away from the programs which we have to come forward with which involve the drawing of lines, setting up of criteria and all the difficulties that come with them.
In other words, we would hope to get away from the ad hoceiy and, of course, to this end there are some very meaningful discussions ongoing. The Grains 2000 group from Winnipeg has put forward some positions for discussion as well as the Department of Agriculture. There have been consultations with the provinces and with many of the leading farm organizations across the country. Certainly it is expected there will be some serious proposals tabled this year with a view to reform of the basic safety net programs, a measure which I am sure Members on all sides, and indeed, all those associated with agriculture will welcome.
I want to just say something in the time remaining in regard to the Canadian Wheat Board. The Board is a trusted and valued institution for producers in western Canada and it is not being undermined in any way. The Wheat Board recently celebrated its fiftieth year in the service of producers within its jurisdiction in what we call the Canadian Wheat Board area in the wheat-growing areas of western Canada. The Board is responsible for export marketing of wheat and barley. It will continue to perform that goal. The Board has helped Canadian producers to establish a reputation for quality grain in the world's market-place.
During the height of the trade war, which I referred to many times, the Board has continued to be able to market grain successfully and to maintain Canada's share in the world market. During the 1987-88 crop year
May 23, 1989

the Board exported a record 31.7 million tonnes of grain, oil seeds and other products. That broke the old record for exports set in the previous year. So, it is clear that the Government stands behind the Canadian Wheat Board.
Last year Bill C-92 was passed which had the effect of strengthening the Canadian Wheat Board by giving greater powers of borrowing and investment to the administrators of the Board. The Government of Canada over the past several years has acted as a backstop for the Board. There was the unfortunate situation of several years ago. The Board basically set the initial prices some 16 months in advance of the end of the crop year of August 31. These were established based on information available at the time which turned out to be overly optimistic with the result that over $300 million of taxpayers' money had to go to the Wheat Board to supplement shortages in the Wheat Board accounts as a result of over-payments made to Canadian producers.
There is also the matter of the sovereign loans made by the Canadian Wheat Board, loans to importing nations, loans which are guaranteed by the Government of Canada. At this time, there is in excess of $3 billion outstanding, and of course, in the event of default, it is not paid by producers but would come out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada.
There is as well the matter of initial prices that are set by Government but on the recommendation of the Canadian Wheat Board. It is the Wheat Board which is in the industry and has sensors around the world. It gives advice on the proper range in which to set the initial prices. Initial prices, of course, are the moneys the farmer receives when he initially delivers his grain to the elevator on the Canadian prairies.
If prices strengthen, there is what is called a final payment. That comes at the end of the crop year and represents the difference between the amount for which the grain is sold by the Canadian Wheat Board and the initial payment which the farmer receives at the elevator. There has been some criticism of the Government because these initial payments are considered too low. I should point out that the Government is relying on the
Supply
advice and expertise of the Canadian Wheat Board when establishing the initial payment levels.
It is the job of the Opposition to criticize, that is fair enough, but surely to do so in a constructive way. Again I have to express some disappointment in that thus far in the course of this Opposition day debate, we have heard a litany of criticism, some warranted and some not, since we do not live in a perfect world, but absolutely no alternatives. I would like to hear, during the course of the Opposition debate, some suggestions as to how things could be made better.
The Government has co-operated and consulted with the producers of Canada as no other Government has before it. We on this side would like to have that same degree of co-operation in an attempt to work together to help Canadian agriculture. I urge Hon. Members opposite to put away the rhetoric and instead to come forward with solid and substantial alternatives in order that we can work together to build a better agricultural economy.
Finally, the Government made the undertaking several years ago to stand solidly behind the farm community of Canada and will continue to do so. The Government is committed to building a strong and vibrant agricultural economy and I believe the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulro-ney) has consistently demonstrated the leadership required to accomplish this end. The Government will continue to show the leadership necessary to fulfil the goals of Canadian agriculture.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACT OF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened very carefully to my hon. colleague from Swift Current-Maple Creek-Assiniboia (Mr. Wilson) and I was pleased to hear him extol the virtues of and to support the Canadian Wheat Board. He spoke of co-operation and of the consultation the Government has engaged in. He exhorted opposition Members to display greater co-operation. Of course, we displayed that co-operation in the last Parliament when practically every government Bill went through in record time or at least all of those that were good Bills. There were a number of bad Bills that took several months or in some cases a year or so to pass. Clearly we are on record as being co-operative with all those good measures and we have already passed one Bill through the House since April.

May 23, 1989
Supply
I would like to question this whole business about consultation. Clearly the dairy farmers of Canada do not think that the consultations they had with regard to the GATT arrangements were adequate. If they did not think the consultations were inadequate, the Chairman of the Ontario Dairy Milk Marketing Commission would not have sent out an urgent letter to every producer demanding its members to immediately get in touch with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Mazankowski) and the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), to try to forestall the crisis which is facing the agricultural industry. If these people had been consulted, they would not have to send out letters like this demanding that the Members call upon the Prime Minister, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister for International Trade as well as federal and provincial MPs. I would question that consultation. I also question the consultation that took place with regard to the removal of oats from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board.
Clearly, the Government had the authority to do that and I do not say that oats needs to be under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board at all times, but clearly no one to whom I have spoken, and I have met with members of all of the prairie pools, feel that they were consulted. I am not simply talking about the advisory committee to the Canadian Wheat Board which may tend to be more supportive of the Wheat Board than those who attend community meetings.
A survey conducted by Decima Research, the polling organization of choice of the Government, the group that tells the Government what to do, shows that 63 per cent were opposed to the decision with regard to oats and only 32 per cent were in favour. As well, 76 per cent felt that there should be more consultation. In spite of what my hon. colleague says, I think there has been a drastic decline in consultation on these issues.
There is one question I would like to put to the Hon. Member. In discussions in the Agriculture Committee, there has been a great deal of support and encouragement for and interest shown in the idea of the production of ethanol from surplus grains or damaged grains, both in eastern Canada and in western Canada. It is very interesting that the executive secretary of the Ontario Com Producers points out in a newsletter to the producers that even though mega-bucks have survived for upgraders, natural gas pipelines to Vancouver, Hibernia and the tarsands project involving many billions of
dollars, there was nothing in the Budget for fuel ethanol development. This is obviously a good method of diversification for the agricultural sector, both in western and in eastern Canada.
The Hon. Member is very close to the Minister of Agriculture. They consult regularly, and I am sure the Hon. Member is aware of the Minister's every idea. Perhaps he could tell us why, in spite of the $5 billion reduction in programs this year and the $9 billion reduction next year, the mega-buck projects survived while there was no incentive provided for fuel ethanol development. Perhaps the Hon. Member could explain exactly what the Government's thinking was in that regard.

Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to unravel further the series of comments on the question. First, I want to say, yes, I do consider myself close to the Deputy Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture, I suspect considerably closer than the Hon. Member might be to some of his front benchers. I am proud to be associated with a Minister of Agriculture who, I believe, has an unsullied reputation of co-operation and consultation with the farm community. I am amazed that the Hon. Member would question the commitment of this Government and indeed its leadership to that sort of consultation and co-operation. Perhaps part of the problem is, as the Member from Etobicoke North (Mr. MacLaren) expressed in an unguarded moment when he said, "From this time forward every sparrow that falls out of the sky will somehow be laid at the feet of the Free Trade Agreement". We are seeing more and more manifestations of that sort of thing. The sparrows are falling out of the sky, and regardless of the cause, they are laid at the feet of that agreement.
I believe that the Hon. Member made mention of the decision taken by the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer) with regard to oats. I can do little other than perhaps repeat to the Hon. Member what the Minister in charge of Grains and Oilseeds said some two weeks ago in the agricultural committee. He said that over the last 40 years oats has become very much a specialty product. It has gone from second or third to something like eleventh in terms of export importance out of the country. It has become very much a special
May 23, 1989

crop because of the volume that we produce, the way it is produced, et cetera. I quote:
We firmly believe that there are more opportunities for individuals out there, smaller companies, the co-operatives, individual seedcleaning plants, farmers-.to process and sell oats to the United States by themselves.
It goes on to talk about the survey that the Hon. Member referred to. I believe it was a Decima survey and apparently on page 12 of that survey it says:
The highest proportion, 41 per cent, believe the pricing of oats through other means will provide higher returns to farmers, 37 per cent believe it will provide lower returns.
That is an interesting commentary. Perhaps you can read anything you like into the results of that type of opinion survey. But the fact is there is a time to consult and there is also a time when a Minister has to make a decision. I know that the Minister in charge of Grains and Oilseeds has criss-crossed western Canada. He has been from one end of the country to the other consulting constantly with producers. It was his judgment, as he has indicated many times, that there was a split decision as far as the removal of oats is concerned. For the reasons that he has outlined many times, he took the decision. I believe that history will prove that he took the right decision.
Finally, I believe the Hon. Member asked the question about ethanol. It came, I believe, from the Member of a Party which has been kind to agriculture over the last 18 to 20 years. This is a Party which visited capital gains tax on Canadian farmers in 1971 at the same time it took away Part 17 capital cost allowance, a Party which brought the LIFT program to western Canada, the Party whose leader said: " Why should I sell your wheat". This is the Opposition who now stand across there purporting and attempting in a feeble way to criticize the outstanding record of this Government over the past four years toward Canadian agriculture.
I am over time, Madam Speaker, and I want to close by saying that there has been a western diversification initiative. Interestingly enough, it is now headed by the same individual as the Minister for Grains and Oilseeds. I am not familiar with every single program and every approval in there, but I would be surprised if there were not initiatives within the western diversification initiative that did not relate to ethanol.

I close, Madam Speaker, by saying that I do not think that the Government needs any lessons in how to deal properly and respectfully with Canadian agriculture. I believe that there has been a record put forward in the last four years which is unmatched in Canadian history. The commitment remains. subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACT OF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must say it is one of the great privileges of being a Member of Parliament from in the Province of Manitoba to have an opportunity to speak on the question of agriculture, an industry which is so dear to the hearts of its people and the one that has traditionally been the mainstay of its economy. In the spirit of the previous speaker, although I think he fell off the wagon near the end about the spirit of goodwill in discussing the problem of agriculture, I remember he too showed frustration with the Government when he stood up a few weeks ago and asked a question in the House about rail abandonment in his constituency. Therefore, it is not only a case of non-partisanship being worried about Government policy, but it us fundamental to the concerns of the people, and it is also about free speech.
My concern as a politician from the City of Winnipeg is in looking out over the countryside and watching year after year the ability of rural Manitoba to stay in existence, to strengthen itself, to build up a strong economy, in gradual decline. Although one would be remiss in simply pointing a finger at one particular Government, the fact that this particular Government has not responded to their needs should be pointed out to the House and discussed by all the Members.
We have heard a lot of facts and figures tossed about today related to the state of our farm economy and the lack of action that this Government has taken. The problem is that this is not an issue that can be dealt with solely in numbers. In fact, we have to take into account some of the human concerns. We have to begin to understand what it means to the people left behind when they see their schools close, when they see themselves lose their health institutions, when they see themselves lose another doctor, lose a dentist, when they see another bus route disappear, a senior citizens home not being built because lack of public money. All these concerns weigh heavily on the people of rural western Canada. Although it is hard to say that one particular program is going to turn things around, it is fair to say that the national agricultural policy continues to

May 23, 1989
Supply
abandon these people. This is a story of people who are struggling against incredible odds and a commodity economy where right now the prices have left them very vulnerable to international trade practices, and therefore has caused a great deal of grief. This is the story of people left behind, of the closing down of rural Canada.
Earlier this year, this Government left 70,000 prairie farmers in limbo over federal drought assistance because they could not get the application forms in in time to prepare adequate submissions before the original deadlines. This is an example of a specific action not taken by the this Government which has created a lot of grief in western Canada. The complexity of this program has not only resulted in delays in getting the forms out. It is also costing an extra $9 million in administration costs over the previous year's program.
This followed an announcement in January by the Minister of Western Economic Diversification and Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer) that initial drought payments would be only 40 per cent to 50 per cent of the total amount due to the farmer. This is in direct contrast to the 70 per cent that this Minister promised during the election last year. One of the great cynicisms that has settled in western Canada is that the Party that has always played up to them, the Party that has always preyed upon the protest somehow finds extra money in an election year. We estimated, for example, the Minister for Western Diversification found $400 million last year. Yet this year he cannot find anywhere near that amount of money. It makes people very cynical of what is happening in western Canada.
These reduced payments have arrived three months later than usual. In the Throne Speech, this Government expressed its concern that agricultural producers were causing "undue pressure to bear on the nation's Treasury". That has become a phrase which has haunted western Canadian farmers since they heard it. As a result of that phrase, they are wondering what does it mean to be an undue pressure on the nation's Treasury. What does it mean to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson)? What does it mean to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Mazankowski) to be an undue burden? What we are finding out year after year-or week after week in this case, but we will find out in the next few years also-exactly what it means to be an undue burden on this
particular Government. It means that the western Canadian farmer is about to suffer.
In the Budget we discovered exactly what kind of measures this Government was prepared to take to relieve this pressure. It has eliminated interest-free commodity-based loans. It has removed $200 million over the next two years from the crop insurance program. It has set higher freight rates while cutting support for branch line rehabilitation. It has attacked the dairy commission. This is on top of a lower initial price for grain, a high interest rate policy maintained by the Government and a declining Canadian market share created by ever-increasing subsidies for producers in Europe and the United States.
What does the future hold for the Canadian farmer? This is the question in front of the House today. The Government on page 65 of its Budget papers has indicated that it will no longer rely on ad hoc programs to aid disaster afflicted farmers even though these programs have the immediacy and the flexibility to best deal with crisis. If there are to be no more ad hoc programs, what plan does the Government have? We feel that the Canadian farmer, and in particular the western Canadian farmer, deserves to hear what these plans are.
Not only has the Government failed to maintain an income- support structure for the Canadian farmer, it has also faded to provide a solution to the farm debt crisis that presents the greatest long-term danger to agricultural production in the country.
One of the greatest hidden statistics in the country, and one that we would like the Government to reveal, is how much acreage in western Canada is now owned by the Canadian banking system. One of the changes that has taken place, and which no one wishes to talk about, is the number of bankruptcies and the inability of Canadian farmers to refinance their operations.For example, the debt of an average prairie farmer in 1986 was thought to be approximately $88,000. That was an increase of $30,000 since 1981. The income available to pay that debt has been dropping. The projected loss in realized net income for a Manitoba farmer will drop by 27.5 per cent. Because of these and other factors, a study done by the Westarc Group, a group working out of
May 23, 1989

western Manitoba, predicts that 4,600 farms will be lost in Manitoba alone over the next seven years.
In Saskatchewan and Alberta, the realized net income will be reduced by 15 per cent. The Saskatchewan pool estimates that 17 per cent of that province's farms are in financial trouble with more than one-half of that number in a non-viable state.
Last year, western farmers paid $7.27 per tonne of grain as their share of transportation costs to get their product to port for export. This year, this share will increase by 24 per cent to an average of $9 per tonne.
A few weeks ago, in various national news reports, the entire country saw the clouds of dust blowing off the fields in Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and Alberta. This is no longer an isolated phenomenon on the Prairies, because it has become widespread and is feared in every comer. A visible dust cloud means a loss of five tonnes per acre of topsoil through soil erosion. This used to be a localized problem in the southern part of the Prairies, but now it is shared by everyone.
Without a strong farm economy, the viability of small towns and even larger centres such as Winnipeg is susceptible to increased pressures and decline. If farmers leave the land, the businesses they support will close or relocate. For example, in St. Anne, Manitoba, there is an unemployment rate of 29.6 per cent; St. Rose du Lac, 21.2 per cent; Neepawa, which is located in the riding of the Minister responsible for western economic diversification, has an unemployment rate of 12.1 per cent. Those rates would be higher if it was not for the sad fact that many young people, who see no future for them in their home towns, leave for places such as Winnipeg, and now beyond to Toronto and Vancouver.
There are community leaders in those towns who have attempted to get assistance from the Government to create jobs, but there has been no help forthcoming. They are not interested in creating megaprojects, but they have realistic plans to employ several people in the manufacturing of unique products that would aid in diversification of the western economy, particularly in small towns. They went to the Department specifically created for that purpose, the Department of the Minister responsible for western economic diversification, but
Supply
they have come back empty handed time and time again. It seems that the Government is more interested in giving millions to multinationals like Boeing than several thousands to a small group in a community such as Roblin.
The Government has not done a proper job in making these programs available to people in rural Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta. An extensive survey of communities and farmers in Manitoba revealed that 50 per cent of people were unaware of any program which offered assistance to those who wanted to start small businesses. In other words, the very people the Government states it wants to help have no idea of the programs available to them. A total of 83 per cent of those surveyed stated that there was a need for the Government to provide better access to information about Government grants and programs available to individuals and communities.
At a series of community meetings held by the Westarc Group in its study of labour market needs in rural Manitoba, it soon became evident that program eligibility requirements that "may be appropriate for urban applicants may be entirely unsuited to the realities of rural Canada and thus thought to discriminate against rural utilization". This was stated by a group that works in Brandon, Manitoba. It is not a group from Winnipeg, Toronto, or a research group from Ottawa. These are the people the Government states it is attempting to help who are speaking out against the Government programs.
They also stated: "The CJS criteria of 42 weeks of unemployment is not applicable to rural areas-traditional unemployment conceptualizations do not have relevance for farmers and thus prevent the needed utilization of CJS benefits in much of rural Manitoba".
The report also stated: "Existing criteria preclude many small businesses having less than the required number of employees from participating and training grants. The majority of rural businesses fit in this category".
Another issue of concern relating to the applicability of Government programs to the rural area is that there are no programs related to the service industry. In urban areas, supporting the service industry is not as much of a

May 23, 1989
Supply
problem, but in the country there is a real need to service the producers who already exist. The same study stated: "The view was expressed that existing programs are geared to manufacturing and processing. Since the majority of business in rural communities is in the service sector, the result is that very little Government programming is available for the small business sector in rural Canada".
How can a farmer survive in rural western Canada if there are not businesses around to deal with, to support, and to give service needed to make a farm a successful enterprise? If those services do not exist, the farmer must travel farther in order to get needed supplies and services. Good weather will not wait while a part is shipped from a regional distributor far away from the farm.
The western Canadian agricultural economy is also affected by the way that international markets have changed in the last 10 years. The United States has decided to pursue an aggressive marketing strategy to get rid of the agricultural surpluses created by its subsidy policy. For example, through the export enhancement program, American exporters receive a free bushel of grain for every three that they can sell. The exporter can do what he likes with this extra bushel, but usually it is built in to the over-all price, giving an automatic subsidy of 25 per cent. At the height of this program, the Americans were giving away one free bushel with every two sold for a subsidy of 33 per cent.
Who is in charge of this system in the United States of subsidies and giveaways? None other than Clayton Yeut-ter, the same U.S. dignitary who is now the Secretary of Agriculture and better known in this country as the architect of the "level playing field" and the Canada-U.S. free trade deal. He did us a great favour.
The European Economic Community is also involved in the subsidy battle. Neither the United States nor the EEC are concerned with managing farm output in the best interests of the producers. They have an open cheque-book policy. The more you grow, the more subsidy you get. This has created a surplus that both these economic units are willing to give away at fire sale prices.
In the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement there is a provision that both countries will sit down to discuss what constitutes a subsidy and what does not. There are 15 specific programs and agencies listed in the Free Trade Agreement as being up for discussion. The Government, more like an admission of guilt than any negotiating strategy or policy position, has already started to eliminate nine of our programs.
Aside from the cuts I have already mentioned, the Government has cut over $396 million from the Estimates for the Agriculture Stabilization Act, Special Grains Program, and the Advance Payments Program. Even though no definition of subsidy has been agreed on, the Government assumes that it is the guilt party. It is not Canada that is subsidizing agricultural exports to the greatest extent in the world, it is other countries. Ministers across the way might try to remember that once in a while. Even if they do not know where they are going, they might think about where they came from.
In conclusion, the Government has failed the western Canadian farmer in many important ways. It has failed to build up the infrastructure needed to ensure production and that support services are there. It has failed to provide job-creation programs of relevance to young people in western Canada. It has failed to maintain income stabilization programs across the West. It has failed in its transportation policies to support the western farmer. Finally, it is failing miserably in negotiating an agreeable situation among our international competitors.

I have a great deal of respect for the hon. gentleman from Willowdale, and have always complimented him. If he could cut through the fog sometimes and get to some very salient points about agriculture, I would probably tend to listen to his rational judgment more than I would to some of the other so-called experts over there.
Let me begin by dealing with The Globe and Mail story that occurred yesterday, I believe, which suggested that the $1 billion grain subsidy was not necessary. It must have been a Liberal who was involved in making that kind of assertion.
I do not know whether other Members have addressed this particular issue, but I think it is worthy of comment.
The article states:
