speechtext:
That does not preclude me from criticizing it. I am fairly open and blunt about things. I want to take issue with this particular conclusion because, quite frankly, if you were to go back and look at the average income in the grains and oilseeds sector from the market-place, the average income was approximately $2.4 billion between 1981 and 1984.
Because of the commencement of the trade war that occurred in 1985, receipts to the grain and oilseeds farmers from the market-place dropped to $1.2 billion, a reduction of approximately 50 per cent. In 1986, it dropped to $945 million and it dropped to $475 million in
Supply
1987. Need I go any further? I am sure hon. colleagues in the House will recognize that that was a very dramatic decline, which was triggered not by this Government but by the vagaries of the market-place and the price war which existed out there.
That brings me to the very important and fundamental point that many Members in the House and others overlook. It is the reliance upon the export market for the viability of our agriculture industry. This country's agriculture industry relies on export markets for about 50 per cent of its sales. That is probably higher than most other countries, and compares to about 20 per cent in the United States.
For example, the Province of Saskatchewan probably gets some 85 per cent of its income from the international market-place; about 80 per cent in the case of Manitoba; and 60 per cent to 70 per cent for Alberta.
What happens in the international market-place is of vital importance to Canadian agriculture, a factor that we sometimes tend to overlook. Whenever there is a price war, wherever there are export restraints, excessive subsidies or quotas, restrictions or trade distortions, our agriculture industry hurts. We must respond to that.
Today we are engaged in that scenario in terms of the approximately $200 billion paid in over-all subsidies toward the global agriculture community. A nation like Canada simply cannot afford to sustain that level of support for an unlimited period.
It is very important to do whatever we can to bring about some order and stability in the market-place. That is why the activities in Geneva, and at the Uruguay Round are very important for the long-term vitality of Canadian agriculture.
We must address the issue of the European common agricultural policy and take what steps we can to bring about a greater degree of reduction in subsidies and export enhancement programs. I think Members opposite should think twice when they suggest that we are selling the shop because we are engaged in dialogue and discussion that will hopefully bring about this kind of order. We know that there are problems.
Reference has been made to the drought situation. Approximately $847 million has been paid out of the crop insurance program, and half of the premiums, about $200 million, are funded by the federal Government. We

May 23, 1989
Supply
are engaged in discussions now with the provinces to try to bring about another formula so that we can achieve two things: a better balance in terms of the equitable cost-sharing program, but also an improved program so that we have a better penetration of the crop insurance program.
When we talk about the need for establishing longterm policies and programs, that is precisely what we are thinking about. We want to establish the kinds of safety nets that will eliminate the necessity of those types of ad hoc programs, whether it be drought assistance to the grain farmer or to the livestock producers.
These are very difficult things to administer, especially when one tries to do it in a fair and equitable way. On every occasion, whether it was the Special Canadian Grains Program or whether it was drought assistance, we have always tried to sit down with the producer groups to work out a mechanism for the payment and distribution of these moneys in a manner that would be consistent with the over-all objectives which they advanced.
That is precisely what we did in the case of the Special Canadian Grains Program. We have done it with respect to the current drought payment which is presently being distributed. If there is any criticism, it would have to be levelled against us for trying to design a program that meets the needs of the producer, to ensure it has sufficient flexibility so that those who are really in need receive and those who are not really in need do not receive. In the past, the programs have been distributed on a broader basis and some who have had good crops still received the drought payment.
We must also consider the importance of recognizing those individuals who buy crop insurance each and every year. Surely there should be some advantage for those who tend to look after themselves.
I am happy to report that we have seemed to reach an all-time high in crop insurance enrolment. Some 85 per cent of producers have enrolled in the Province of Saskatchewan, about 70 per cent in the Province of Manitoba and 50 per cent in the Province of Ontario, which I believe is higher than usual. Some 60 per cent of producers have enrolled in Quebec, 75 per cent in Alberta, and 65 per cent in British Columbia, for a total of 144,000 producers who have enrolled, an average of 68
per cent across the country. That compares with 132,250 in 1988.
It is also important to note that in terms of precipitation and temperature, the accumulated precipitation deficit taken at the Lethbridge, Alberta Station shows that the deficiency in rainfall was much more severe in the last period, 1979-88 than between the years 1929 and 1939. As well, in terms of average mean temperatures, the temperatures were higher between 1979-88 than they were between 1929-38. That really tells us that the drought conditions were much more severe during this period of time than they were during the so-called dirty thirties.
I would like to return to the drought payments and refer to the latest statistics that we have. There are 57,730 cheques in the mail for a total of $214 million. As my colleague the Minister responsible has indicated, the payments are going out. We expect that the final payments should be in the mail some time during the month of July.
When we look at the level of assistance that has been provided by the Government and when we look at the realized net income, we see that in spite of all the hardship-the drought and the collapse in commodity prices-we still end up with some rather interesting figures. In 1988, the realized net income for farmers across Canada reached $5.2 billion. That is the highest on record. In 1987, that figure was $4.7 billion. In 1986, it was $4.2 billion. In 1985, it was $3.8 billion. There has been a steady progression of roughly around 30 per cent to 35 per cent.
We recognize that in some quarters that may not be seen as enough. However, when we consider that the federal Government alone put in $6.1 billion of income support to the farm community in 1988, and when we consider that the over-all net realized income was $5.2 billion, we quickly realize that the federal Government has put in more than has been realized in terms of net income. That does not strike me as a Government that is uncaring. It does not strike me as a Government that has turned its back on farmers. The fact of the matter is we have not turned our back on the farmers. When it comes to supporting Canadian agriculture, the Government's record is unsurpassed by any other Government since I
May 23, 1989

have been around this institution. The figures will bear me out on that.
There can be criticisms of whether we were effective enough, or whether there was fair and equitable distribution. Whenever we look at ad hoc programs we see that the difficulty is that there is a tendency from time to time, because all the elements may not be weighed, for charges to be made of discrimination between commodities. There are charges that one region is being treated better than another. That is what happens when we get into the responses to individual problems that occur. This is one of the reasons we are going through the policy review.
We are trying to establish a new policy framework based upon the success or failure rate of any existing policy. We also want to put in place, hopefully, a regime that will provide some permanence, some confidence, some stability and some security, whether it is in the area of safety nets, stabilization, crop insurance, farm financing, research and development, marketing or the strengthening and modification of our agriculture marketing boards. This will ensure that the farmers can take advantage of the opportunities out there. All these things are under review based upon the experiences that we have had over the last four or five years. I think that is eminently sensible. It seems to me that that is one of the things that should be done from time to time.
We have a situation, whether we like it or not, where our international trading environment is in a bit of turmoil. That is a fact of life. However, we hope that this will be resolved at some point in time. We have to be positioned in such a way that we take advantage of those new trading opportunities. Our goal is to maintain and secure what we have today in terms of our market penetration, but also to try to ensure that we can position ourselves in such a way that we can further enhance the opportunities for international trade, given the importance that we place upon trade and the future of Canadian agriculture.
I heard a great many things about the Budget. We are all aware of the difficulties we have, as a nation, in terms of our fiscal position. We have heard it said many times that the cost of servicing the debt consumes about 35 cents of every taxpayer's dollar that we collect. So it is an issue we must address.

As I said, when it comes to supporting Canadian farmers and the agri-food industry, our Government has a proud record which I believe is unsurpassed.
During the previous four years the federal Government invested some $17 billion in agriculture. That is more than double the previous four-year period.
We have stood behind agriculture, behind farmers and the industry associated with it, because it is an important industry. It is about a $22 billion megaproject in terms of direct gross income to the farmers across the country. Those are big dollars and the multiplier effect, depending on who we listen to, is four or five. It does generate about 10 per cent of our GNP. It earns billions of dollars in export earnings, and it is a very important way of life.
We have extended a helping hand to the agriculture industry when it was in need. I do not think that farmers expect so-called hand-outs when they can fend for themselves. What we are looking at now are programs and policies that would allow them to become more self-reliant.
We are looking at programs and policies that are in place so that they can make market decisions based upon the reality of the market-place, but at the same time, on a set of policies and programs that are announced and that are clearly established. I believe it is very difficult for them to make decisions on the basis of not knowing for sure whether they are going to get a drought relief program, or whether they are going to get a special Canadian grains program. Or when the stabilization program goes belly-up, whether the Government of the day can provide the necessary money to replenish it. Those are some of the challenges that we have had to go through. It has been a very serious time but we have responded in a period where we have been attempting to bring the deficit into line.

When we look at some of the facts, the family owned farm enterprise is quite alive and well in Canada, contrary to the views expressed here in this House. The allegation that they are being gobbled up by
huge large-scale agri-businesses is not true. The family farm business still represents about 99 per cent of Canada's agricultural production units. The ratio of debts to assets is marginally higher than it was just 25 years ago.

First, the price has to fall below 10 per cent of what it was in a five-year average. Second, that price must be down a full five days before this tax can even come into effect. Third, the sum average of Canadian acreage under vegetables or the soft fruits must not have

We have been involved in agriculture matters for quite some time and in fact we have put forth a very practical and veiy logical agricultural policy during the last campaign.
Agriculture, as the Hon. Minister indicated, is an important part of the economic fabric of this nation. It contributes some 10 per cent of the GNP in this country, it employs well over half a million people, and at this time there are some 300,000 family farms in Canada. Unfortunately, that number is down from a high of 723,000 farms in 1941.
I would like to widen this debate slightly if I could. While agriculture is important, there is also the entire rural infrastructure of this country that is also important. We have not only family farms but we have small towns and communities that are an integral part of the agriculture community. We have small businesses, everything from implement dealerships to general stores. We have services such as doctors, hospitals and lawyers who are part of the whole rural infrastructure. We have services such as senior citizens' homes. Infrastructures are interdependent upon each other, each facet is interdependent upon the other.
The problem with this whole rural infrastructure is that since World War II it has been coming under increasing pressure and stress. Certainly the size of the
Supply
average family farm has increased dramatically. We have less than half the number of family farms that we had in the 1940s and part of that, of course, is due to technological advancement. Certainly the days of the 160-acre farm are gone, and so they should be with the horse-drawn days and the long hard days of back-breaking work which has been replaced by significant technological advancements. However, there is another aspect to this entire demise that is starting to take place with respect to the rural infrastructure in Canada. Successive Governments since the Second World War have done little to encourage the survival of family farms and rural infrastructure generally.
The fact that Governments have done little says a lot about the Government's overall attitude toward agriculture. This care-not attitude has been clear since the Government was elected in 1984. Government Members talk of the billions of dollars the Government has put toward agriculture and that is true, it has, but unfortunately, the money has gone largely to ad hoc programs, programs that are ill-conceived and do not promote the family farm and rural infrastructure generally. These programs have been designed to promote election victories for successive Conservative Governments.
The Government's win-a-vote policy is best exemplified by the so-called drought relief program announced some 11 days before the last federal election. As early as August of last year, farmers knew that drought was a serious matter in rural Canada and the Government promised a drought relief program. In fact, in 1985, it promised a permanent drought relief program but it has yet to deliver on that promise.
Just 11 days before the election, the Government announced that $850 million would go to support farmers suffering from drought. This program was announced for political purposes. There was no indication of how it would be paid out. It was simply announced that $850 million would be provided, and government Members proceeded to state that farmers in the extensively hit areas of drought would receive up to $45 per acre. Doing the calculations, it becomes pretty obvious that if all farmers in the severely drought stricken areas would receive $45 per acre, the final amount would be far in excess of $850 million.

I felt sorry for my Conservative opponent during the election campaign. Ele had extreme difficulty, with justification, trying to explain the program. He could not do it because there were no details announced.
When the House reconvened in December, Members on this side of the House asked the Government when we could expect a drought payment. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Mazankowski) indicated that we could expect forms out within 10 days. Government Members had indicated earlier that final payments would be out in early January. January came and went and there were no forms and no payments.
Then government Members said that they would have the final payments out by seeding time because farmers needed money during seeding time so they could put their seed in the ground. Seeding time has come and gone and the final payments are not out. The application forms are out and money is starting to come in. Now government Members are saying that funds will be out in July because farmers need money to purchase the chemicals that they spray.
At an agriculture committee meeting not too long ago, the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer) was present. One of the Minister's experts indicated that in fact, final payments would come some time after July. Now I suppose government Members will be saying that the payments will come out during harvest time because farmers need money during harvest time.
It is clear that this program was ill conceived. It was simply announced for political purposes. The unfortunate part of the program is that it was ad hoc and ill conceived. The Government is now promising a permanent program. I hope that it will finally come through with that program. Certainly, it has been saying it would since 1985. The other concern of Members on this side of the House is that when that program is finally unleashed on the Canadian public, we hope that it will be aimed at maintaining family farms or rural communities and will not simply be a product of big agri-business with its interests at heart.
The Minister indicated earlier that there have been increased profits in agriculture in recent years, and that is true. That cannot be denied. The other fact is that there are record debts in agriculture. Over $24 billion in farm debt exists in Canada today. Communities are
closing and the Government is about to inflict a neoconservative policy on the nation.
While there have been record returns, there have also been record numbers of farms going bankrupt. What is happening is very clear. We are starting to develop an economic class structure within rural communities. There are a few farms that are becoming larger and more successful and a great many family farms that are struggling to survive. Despite the amount of money that has been thrown at past programs, it has not fallen in the right places. The programs have not been well thought out.
It is clear that the Minister will come through with a program for agriculture, but we on this side of the House are concerned about what kind of program it will be. This Government prides itself on consultation. It says it consults with all groups and listens well. Unfortunately, it listens better to certain segments than to others. We can best see that with respect to the Canadian Wheat Board.
Back in February, the Government announced that oats would be removed from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. The Government said that farmers wanted this and had been consulted on it. The Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds indicated that he had received hundreds of letters from producers across Canada who were in favour of removing oats from the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board, and he said that he consulted with farm groups. The reality is that some consultation was undertaken but it was not wide consultation.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture passed a unanimous resolution calling on the Government not to remove oats from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board without allowing western Canadian producers to vote on it. The Government has ignored that. It has ignored calls from the prairie wheat pools. Certainly the Saskatchewan and Manitoba wheat pools have called for no removal of oats without a producer vote.
The Government has ignored the comments and advice of the advisory committee to the Canadian Wheat Board. The advisory committee is composed of members duly elected by some 135,000 permit book holders from across western Canada. These members were elected to advise the Government on Wheat Board matters but the Government ignores them.
May 23, 1989

Who did the Government listen to? The Government will say that the United Grain Growers and the Western Canadian Wheat Growers Association agrees with the policy and that is fair because these groups include oats producers. However, government Members will go on to include the Alberta Sheep and Wool Commission, the Alberta Pork Producers, the Saskatchewan Pork Marketing Board, the Western Barley Growers Association and the Canadian Cattlemen's Association. I am not sure how many of those groups are composed of actual producers, but those associations do not produce oats. The advisory committee to the Canadian Wheat Board should have more to say about the future of the Canadian Wheat Board than the Alberta Sheep and Wool Commission.
When oats was removed from the Canadian Wheat Board, it was indicated there was only some 1 per cent. That 1 per cent represents $300 million to the Canadian economy, and more particularly to wheat board producers. We can see that the Government did not listen, that wide consultation did not take place. The Decima poll has been referred to here today which was released by producers. In fact, the Decima poll is the polling authority that the Government uses all the time. It indicated that some 62 per cent wished oats to remain on the Canadian Wheat Board and that some 31 per cent were opposed to it, and a full two-thirds were producers.
The Government will respond that approximately 41 per cent of producers believe that oats produced outside the Wheat Board will receive higher returns. The producers who believe that oats inside the Wheat Board will receive high returns is 37 per cent. It is a virtual saw. If Government Members would look at the poll, they would see that it states that prairie farmers are unwilling to give up the security of marketing oats through the Wheat Board. While they recognize that there may be other means of marketing which would provide higher returns, they appear to sense a comfort level with the Canadian Wheat Board which will be lost as a result of the federal Government's decision. There is a risk attached to change, and respondents are not convinced that the risk is worth-while even if it means higher returns. The reliability and security which the Wheat Board provides is an important factor for farmers when considering the removal of some grains.

It is very clear, Mr. Speaker, that producers in western Canada want the Wheat Board, and this Government simply has refused to listen to the majority of those producers. Another example of this Government's attitude toward agriculture in this country is clearly seen with respect to the Budget. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) indicated earlier that agriculture in this country is improving. Perhaps the Minister of Finance should have a chat with the Minister of Agriculture who just a moment ago indicated that average rainfall is now less than it was in the thirties. Perhaps if they exchanged some information, the Minister of Finance would not make those remarks. Perhaps the Minister of Finance should take a trip to Saskatchewan. Maybe he should take a trip to the Estevan area where recently there have been high winds of such an extent that farmers are having to re-seed, some for the second time. Perhaps he should visit the community of Rosetown where there is a severe drought or how about Davidson or Watrous where producers are suffering.
The Finance Minister says that the West is recovering. Certainly the drought is still in existence. Certainly world prices have not come up. Yet we have a Minister premising his remarks with respect to cuts in agriculture with the fact that agriculture is on the mend. The Government will be coming forth, we believe, with proposals this summer, with a plan, and it will be a wide, extensive plan with respect to agriculture and with respect to the whole infrastructure of rural Canada. It is going to affect everything from transport to seed production to purchase of grains. It is going to be a program that will have a tremendous affect on the future of this nation.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Mazankowski) indicated that the Government is not turning its back on family farms. He indicated there was more to agriculture than simply growing grain and the economics of agriculture. In fact, it is a way of life, and that is true. I certainly hope the Minister in putting forth the proposals will consider that way of life. I, and those of us on this side of the House, have real concerns with respect to that. We have concerns that in fact the Government has the ear of companies such as Cargill and Canadian Pacific, companies which are not concerned with the future of the family farm, companies which are concerned simply with making a profit, companies which are concerned with the bottom line. That bottom line does not measure into the way of life for rural Canada. There are factors that simply cannot be measured. This is a Government that

May 23, 1989
Supply
has to philosophically decide whether it wants to simply look at the bottom line or whether it wants to maintain a viable rural infrastructure that includes not only family farms but businesses and all the services that exist within that entire structure.
When that program comes out, and hopefully it will come out this summer, we look forward to having a good opportunity to address it, to put forth observations. We hope that the Government will in fact take a wide range approach.
Certainly thus far it has not. When the Government talks about the number of groups that are in favour of its program so far, there is one thing these groups have in common. This is certainly true with respect to groups that were in favour of oats being removed from the Wheat Board. As I indicated before, the Alberta Sheep and Wool Commission has had very little to do with the production of oats. But what the Alberta Sheep and Wool Commission, the hog producers and the Cattlemen's Association have in common is that these are the very groups that agree with the Government's position. These are the very groups that sponsored an ad during the recent election campaign in support of free trade. These are the groups that have one mind. This is one aspect, one view of the future of agriculture. The Government should open its ears and eyes and pay more attention to the rest of the producers. Certainly it should not be taking such a narrow view. Certainly it should be listening to the producers. It is very clear from the Decima poll and from other groups in this country that there is another view.
It is our hope and concern that when new programs are developed, and we welcome a permanent drought relief program and new measures in agriculture, that producers in western Canada, and across the rest of this nation, should have a say as to which direction this Government is going and simply not listen to the big agri-business and the Cargills and the Canadian Pacifies of this world.

This is a Government that is not the friend of supply management. That is for sure. This is a Government that is going to undermine supply management where it can. Unfortunately, it will use international trading negotiations as an excuse. Certainly, the problems with industrial milk are only one example.
There is another example with respect to the Canadian Wheat Board. When the initial prices came out recently for the Canadian Wheat Board, they were lower than most producers expected. Prices for grain were very low. Ihking into account the fact that the world price of grain is still low, the amounts of grain that are in reserve are down. As a result, grain prices were expected to rise dramatically. Yet, the announcement by the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer) indicated that initial prices were very low. The reason is simply that the Americans do not appreciate the Canadian Wheat Board. They do not like the benefit it brings to the Canadian producers. They are trying to effectively handcuff the Canadian Wheat Board. By making prices lower they are taking money out of the pockets of producers when they deliver the grain to the terminals. It is strictly the result of American pressure to bring lower initial prices with respect to the Canadian Wheat Board. There
May 23, 1989

is example after example with respect to that in supply management.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACT OF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
I would like the Hon. Member to take a moment and comment upon the things that the Government has done. I am sure he would have to agree that what the Government has done sends a very strong signal of the support the Government has for supply management. In particular, I would like him to comment on the implementation of quotas for hatching eggs and chicks.
I would also like the Hon. Member's comments on the dairy industry. In particular, last year there was a time when the price of milk could have been reduced. That happened again in February this year. The Government, in consultation with the dairy industry, did not do that. In the wisdom of the Canadian Dairy Commission and the Government it was decided not to lower those prices. There is nothing to say that when those prices are reviewed again that the prices should increase. That does not mean that the Government is not supporting the supply management sectors. As a Government we have done many things in support, in the last Parliament as well as since we have returned after the last election. We have shown strong support, in particular with respect to the implementation of the quotas on hatching eggs and chick marketing imports.
I would like the Hon. Member to comment on those two items.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACT OF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
With respect to dairy products, the Government has frozen industrial milk prices for some 20 months. That action, coupled with $14 million in budget cuts, will hurt dairy farmers. The National Association of Dairy Farmers of Canada has expressed its concern in news releases and in personal communications with the Minister. The current price of a hectolitre of industrial milk is approximately $47. It is often expressed as $47.06, if carrying charges are included.
Supply
When the Minister for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer) appeared before the committee on May 10, he stated that even though the formula should have triggered two decreases in the past year, the Government did not lower the industrial milk price. I have seen this same argument expounded in information that the Government released. The DFC refutes this. First the Government states that last August the formula should have triggered a decrease of $1.89. That is the formula without indexation. DFC has stated that the Government contention is irrelevant because the costs have not been indexed forward. If it had been indexed, the price would have been unchanged at $46.93 at hectolitre.
Second, the Government stated that the formula should have triggered a 14-cent decrease. The Government is using an average of the last four quarters when DFC states it should use the last quarter only. If that had been done, the formula would have triggered an increase of 2.9 cents. Besides, the whole matter is irrelevant because there has to be at least a 2 per cent change in the formula to trigger an increase or a decrease. The DFC and the Government's calculation is very clear. Mark Twain had a saying that figures don't lie but liars figure. It is simple to take figures and programs and use them for one's own purpose. This is what the Government has done in the past.
I am not denying that the Government, has not had some programs which have benefited agriculture. The problem is to a large extent programs have been put forth with a feeling not for the future of agriculture, but simply with political opportunism in mind. That is the aspect we have been checking when looking at the programs of the Government.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACT OF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
I would like to pick up on the thought of the Hon. Member for Huron-Bruce (Mr. Cardiff). I would like to suggest that the Government has taken every opportunity to support the supply management system here in Canada.
First, in looking at the dairy industry, last February yoghurt and ice cream were put on the import control list. That was clearly to support the dairy industry in this country. As the Member for Huron-Bruce stated, more recently the broiler chicks and hatching eggs board was established and the borders were closed for those panic-

Supply
ular commodities. Again, that is a significant step to support the concept of supply management here in Canada.
We are now at a stage in the GATT discussions where the importance of Article 11 in supporting supply management is under discussion. As I said, that is at a very critical stage. The Canadian Government and the negotiators for the Government want to go into those discussions in the strongest position possible. It is important that Canada appear to be clean in these discussions.
I would ask the Member what he would suggest, or what his Party would do to strengthen the position of the Canadian negotiators involved in these multilateral trade negotiations. Certainly, the cap was put on for one reason only, and that was to strengthen the Canadians' bargaining position for the long-term support of supply management; to maintain, to clarify, and to strengthen Article 11 which is one of the major underpinnings of supply management here in Canada. If we do not appear to be clean, what would the Member suggest we do?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACT OF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to talk about something veiy close to my heart, Canadian agriculture. I especially appreciate the occasion to look at the farm situation in Ontario, the province with the largest and most diversified agricultural sector. I particularly relish relating to the House the Government's record in supporting the industry and in
laying the ground work for its long-term prosperity both in Ontario and across the nation.
Too often over the past few years the House has heard how bad it is down on the farm; depressed grain prices, bad weather, financial difficulties, drought. I should not need to remind Members that this Government has responded in an unprecedented way. We came forward with a program to buffer grain and oilseed producers across the country from the savage effects of an insane international trade war.
We have been working hard at the international level to put the brakes to this subsidy. There has been significant progress and Canada has been no small partner in that effort.
On the home front, we have helped individual farmers faced with financial difficulties come to new arrangements with their creditors. Innovative farm debt review boards have been a resounding success, helping many producers and their families stay on the farm.
Unfortunately, the weather has played hard ball these last few seasons but this Government has gone to bat for Canadian farmers. In 1986 we paid out over $200 million to help western farmers through a serious dry spell. In late 1987, the signs were back of severe drought in several parts of the country, including Ontario.
In early 1988, in co-operation with provinces, we announced assistance programs for green feed and livestock. Last fall we announced a major Canadian crop drought assistance program. First payments have been made and final payments are being determined.
It is true there has been bad news in agriculture these past years, but the federal Government has done more than its fair share to assist farmers.
The long-term dairy policy announced in January, 1986, ensured stability to an important agricultural sector, one that is worth $1 billion a year in Ontario alone. This Government's commitment to the dairy sector and the concept of supply management remains as firm as ever.
One area of particular interest to the Province of Ontario is how we have helped the tobacco industry adjust to new times and the decline in domestic demand. Working with the province, we set up several assistance programs. The federal Government has committed $45 million to the Ontario Assistance Program. This pro-
May 23, 1989

gram has two objectives. The first is to assist producers wishing to leave the tobacco growing industry. The second is to help rationalize the industry so that remaining producers can become more viable.
In addition, there is the Alternate Enterprise Initiative. This is another joint program with the province, worth almost $14 million. The program is designed to provide start-up funding for tobacco growers wishing to leave tobacco production for another crop.
The initiative focuses on alternate market development, alternate crop development and research.
Funding has been for projects involving a variety of crops including peanuts, cash crop hay, ginseng, evening primrose, onions, garlic, sweet potatoes and strawberries.
Over-all, it is an excellent example of how this Government has taken seemingly bad news of depressed prices and markets and turned it into a success story. Time and time again, we have managed this by working closely in partnership with the provinces and by relying on the initiative and drive of Canadian producers to adapt and compete.
It is that initiative and competitiveness which gave us complete confidence in reaching an accord on trade with the United States of America. The signing of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement was good news indeed for Canadian producers. I know that our agrifood sector is eager to take on the Americans on their home turf.
We have provided Canadian farmers with an extraordinary opportunity, the chance to compete unfettered in a market of over 240 million consumers.
A recent trade seminar at the University of Michigan heard that Canada and Ontario stand to gain the most from the agreement. Ontario farmers can expect to ship more products across the border, and will likely sell more vegetables in major markets like Detroit.
For example, opportunities will be created with the reduction and elimination of the 25 per cent tariffs on broccoli and brussel sprouts and the 12.5 per cent duty on cauliflower entering the United States. Enhanced
Supply
access to the American market will also benefit floriculture, a growth industry that is in an enviable position to exploit the new market. Ontario $5.5 billion agriculture sector can only get bigger and stronger with opportunities like that at its doorstep. It is one major reason why there is renewed optimism in the crop and pasture lands, in the feed lots and packing plants, the greenhouses and berry fields. Things are not nearly as bad as yesterday's sensational headlines would have us believe.
Just look at the latest results from the Reid monthly survey. In April, Reid looked at how Canadian farmers assess their financial situation. The pollster found that there has been a marked improvement in Canadian farmers' outlook since the last such survey was undertaken two years ago. Farmers are feeling confident and upbeat. Reid noted that Ontario farmers are feeling particularly positive about how their operation did last year. This may be surprising to some, especially those who would believe that our agriculture sector is weak and not able to compete. But I am not surprised.
I believe the Canadian agri-food sector is more vibrant and resilient than it is often given credit. In fact, the present real picture in agriculture is considerably different than that painted by the media and those interested in portraying the family farm as a thing of the past.
I think it is important that we begin to set the record straight on a few current notions about the state of Canadian farming. It is true that our farm population has declined over the years. It was 11 per cent of the population in 1961 and was just 3.5 per cent in 1986. But rural Canada is still alive. The non-farm rural population has been stable at around 20 per cent. Total employment in agriculture has remained fairly constant since the early 1970s.
Although farm numbers are down, those farms with sales of $50,000 and more have actually increased. In fact, since 1981 there are 29,000 more farms with annual sales over $50,000.
Larger farms tend to be more viable. Almost two-thirds of farms with annual sales over $100,000 show little risk of failure.

Supply
In spite of the trend to larger farms, the family-owned farm remains the basic unit of agricultural production in Canada. Non-family corporations account for less than one-half of 1 per cent of Canadian farms.
We hear a lot about the farm debt situation. It is true that high levels of debt have been seen as a major problem facing agriculture. Farm debt grew from $2 billion in 1961 to $5 billion in 1971. In the next ten years, it jumped to $18 billion as a result of increased capital borrowing in the mid-1970s, in response to strong commodity prices.
When interest rates rose to historically high levels in 1981 and remained there for several years, many highly leveraged farmers found themselves in financial difficulty. But while farm debt shot up, so did the value of farm assets. In 1988, the ratio of debts to assets was only slightly higher than in the early 1970s.
Low commodity prices in some sectors, high input costs and the world trade situation would lead most of us to believe that farm incomes have been seriously affected.
The evidence cited for this is the decline in aggregate real farm income, which is well below the levels of the past two decades. However, aggregate income does not not take into account declining farm numbers and increased income support earned off the farm. When you compare income earned by farm families to that of other Canadian families, Madam Speaker, you will see that they are about the same.
These things suggest that the financial position of farmers may not be as bad as many people assume. I have of course spoken about aggregate numbers. I did this to indicate to Hon. Members that the over-all current financial state of Canadian agriculture is good.
Of course, there will always be exceptions. In those cases the federal Government will continue to provide the tools necessary for the survival and prosperity of viable operations. The Government believes in the farmers of Canada. It believes in their ability to compete in Canada, in the U.S. and offshore as well. It believes in their initiative, their self-reliance and their perennial optimism. We believe in their desire to succeed and to hold on to their rural values as they take up the latest in technological improvements.
Finally, we believe in the farmers of Canada because the farmers of Canada believe in themselves. We as a Government look forward to working with the farmers of Canada in the future to improve the future of agriculture in this great country.

Madam Speaker, I am wondering if the Hon. Member would like to comment on the price discovery mechanism in the world grain markets in view of the scandals that have taken place in New York markets and the Chicago commodity markets and also in regard to the investigations going on in the Winnipeg grain market as outlined by the Hon. Member for Mackenzie (Mr. Althouse) in this debate today.
What are the Hon. Member's thoughts as to the future of the Canadian Wheat Board when the subsidy levels between Canada and the United States become level and there is free movement of grain between the two countries.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACT OF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member mentioned the Wheat Board. There seems to be a myth that the Government under the direction of the Minister of Agriculture is attempting to harm the Wheat Board. We are not attempting to harm the Wheat Board. We are attempting, as we do in all areas of agriculture, to strengthen the position of agriculture in Canada thereby allowing Canadian farmers to compete all across Canada, the United States and the world. The Government is out to protect Canadian farmers and to strengthen their position in this country.
The Hon. Member asked about Winnipeg grain futures and world prices. When we look at world prices we realize that that is what we as a Government are attempting to look at through the GATT round of negotiations. That is to say we wish to consider the support that other countries are giving their farmers which makes it impossible for us to compete. The Government is attempting through negotiations under the GATT round to see that in the future subsidies in agriculture will not make it impossible for Canadian farmers to compete.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACT OF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member mentioned subsidies being used by other countries. He will be aware that moments before the initialling of the Canada-U.S. Trade Agreement the U.S. administration of the day extended the use of its export enhancement program some time into the 1990s. In spite of clauses in the agreement which appeared to protect ourselves and the Americans from each other's programs like the
May 23, 1989

export enhancement program they interpreted their action as having been taken before the agreement was signed and therefore should continue on for some time.
This morning our Minister of Agriculture met with the American Secretary of State for Agriculture. Can the Hon. Member for Elgin (Mr. Monteith) perhaps qualify why it is that we now hear our government Members in the form of the Minister of Agriculture appear to approve of the American use of export enhancement subsidies into traditional markets of Canada in spite of what we thought was an agreement whereby they would not do that to us and we would not do it to them?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACT OF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we in Canada recognize that we have to compete worldwide in agriculture. We hope to promote not only trade with the United States but trade with many other countries. We hope that all our commodity groups look to increased trade with the United States. That is what the bilateral agreement with the U.S. promotes. The opportunity for Canadian farmers and business to continue with the amount of trade that we have with the United States is an opportunity to enhance that trade by going into more markets. They will be assisted by Governments helping them to market their product throughout the United States and other countries.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACT OF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is clear from the debate today that the Government is keeping its commitment to Canadian farmers, and continues in a number of ways to keep that commitment. One way, of course, is by continuing to support the role of supply management agencies. In addition to that no Government in history has done as much for agriculture as has this one since 1984. There is heartfelt, sincere and determined support for agriculture. The Government remains open to constructive suggestions and comments that will help us together build Canadian agriculture.
In terms of the job assistance program, no government program is perfect. There can always be improvements. The Government has responded as quickly as reasonably possible in a manner that is fair. It has listened to producers in preparing the program.
Borrowing Authority
I suggest that if there is to be condemnation today in the House, which the motion calls for, then that condemnation should be reserved for those Members opposite who seek to scare Canadian farmers about their own future. Canadian farmers have a tremendous future. The Government continues to stand behind them in many ways through drought assistance and other programs. We continue to fight on their behalf in international marketplaces through GATT and other measures. I suggest that the Government, unlike any other Government in history, has stood behind Canadian agriculture.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ALLEGED IMPACT OF GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member has indicated that Canadian farmers support the Government. They support us because of the fact that we have supported agriculture. We support supply management. We have been there when the farmers were in need.
The fact that there has been an increase in graduates and enrolment in agricultural colleges and universities all across the country of 150 per cent tells us that there is confidence in agriculture. That confidence has come about because of the policies of the Government.
